title: AisleLens Coffee Standard v1.0 — buyer questions, assertions and evidence rules for roasted coffee product pages

posture.statement: This document has never been applied to a real store by anyone, and no second party has applied it without us. Until that happens it is a rubric with a versioned changelog, not a standard. It is written to a publishable bar and is not published. Every failure rate in it is a prediction, not a measurement. The independently_applied flag may only become true once a second party has run this document without the authoring party's involvement.

applicability_envelope.covers: Retail product pages selling roasted coffee to consumers as whole bean, ground, pods or capsules, including decaffeinated coffee, single-origin lots and blends.
excludes: green (unroasted) coffee, whose grading and admissibility rules differ materially
instant, extract and chicory-blend products governed by separate compositional rules
coffee-flavoured goods that are not coffee (syrups, confectionery, scented products)
flavoured coffee, for the ingredient and allergen entries only, which are blocked rather than applied

never: tags — a coffee-scented soap must never read as a coffee product, which is the engine's own rule at src/server/productTest.ts:877-884
collection handles and URL slugs, which are merchant-controlled naming rather than evidence

out_of_scope.subject: whether any claim on the page is true
out_of_scope.why_not: The engine adjudicates evidence availability, never product truth. Every assertion here answers whether a statement of a defined form is published and readable, and none of them answers whether the coffee is what the page says it is.

out_of_scope.subject: health, wellbeing and physiological effects of coffee
out_of_scope.why_not: Health and structure/function claims are separately regulated in every major market and substantiation attaches to whoever makes the claim. A standard that adjudicated 'boosts focus' or 'low acid, gentler on your stomach' would be taking a position on a regulated claim, which is exposure this document must not walk into.

out_of_scope.subject: environmental and ethical-sourcing claims that name no scheme
out_of_scope.why_not: Unqualified general environmental benefit claims are the target of active regulation rather than a category to score. Recording the presence of 'sustainably sourced' or 'carbon neutral' as conformance would invert the law, because presence is the risk factor and not the evidence.

out_of_scope.subject: sensory quality, tasting notes and cup preference
out_of_scope.why_not: There is no external definition a third party could check a flavour descriptor against, so an assertion over tasting notes would degrade the test into confirming that adjectives are present.

out_of_scope.subject: the physical label on the bag that will arrive
out_of_scope.why_not: Several of the strongest coffee facts — the roast date, the net quantity declaration, the certifier name — are lot-level and printed at pack time. A page-level test can only ever confirm that a claim about the label was made, never that the delivered bag carries it.

out_of_scope.subject: price fairness, value for money and producer payment levels
out_of_scope.why_not: Farmgate price, premium paid and direct-trade terms have no register, no definition and no public record; the main price-transparency reference in coffee is anonymised aggregate data by construction and cannot confirm any individual contract.

changelog.summary: First authored version. Ten executable assertions, five deliberately not executed on discrimination grounds, sixteen blocked on engine capability, thirteen advisory. Nothing has been measured against a real store.

changes.rationale: Whole-bean versus ground is the delivered physical state, is a mandatory part of the name of the food in the EU, and is the format decision a buyer most often gets wrong.
Organic is the only coffee claim that is simultaneously mandated on-label, resolvable to the seller in a free public register, and status-typed, so it anchors the certification class.

Published as not_discriminating rather than executable: the engine's own note records that this row returns a passing state unless a hard subscription blocker is found, so it would fire for almost nobody.
Growing country is the most commercially central coffee claim and has no engine mechanism at all, so it is published as blocked with the reasoning rather than omitted.

entries.question: Can I buy this as whole beans?

applicability.applies_when: the product is roasted coffee sold by mass rather than in pods or capsules
does_not_apply_when: the product is a pod, capsule or pre-dosed sachet, where the state is inherent to the format
applicability.signal: product_type or title indicates coffee; pod and capsule products are excluded by the envelope

accepted_evidence.form: a purchasable option value naming the whole-bean state
the matching variant is listed and marked available

insufficient_evidence.form: "beans" as a generic synonym for coffee
insufficient_evidence.why_not: "our house beans" and "single origin beans" are marketing register, not a statement about the delivered state; a product literally named Bean Blend can ship ground.

insufficient_evidence.form: an option LIST containing whole bean among others
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A page offering Whole Bean / Espresso / Filter asserts none of them about what ships. This entry asks only whether the option is purchasable, which is the narrower and answerable question.

insufficient_evidence.form: "freshly ground" or "we grind to order"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: These state a process the seller performs, not the state of this purchasable item, and in some sellers' usage they describe what the buyer is expected to do.

insufficient_evidence.form: a photograph of beans, a grinder or a portafilter
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Image content is not page text, is not read by the engine, and bean photography is routinely used as brand imagery on ground products.

insufficient_evidence.form: a brew-method mention such as "excellent in a French press"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: This implies a target grind and says nothing about whether the bag contains beans.

conflict_rules.when: the title says whole bean and no whole-bean option is purchasable
conflict_rules.resolution: the purchasable option list decides; a title is not an offer

conflict_rules.when: a whole-bean option exists but is out of stock
conflict_rules.resolution: report it as listed and not purchasable, which is what the engine returns, rather than as absent

registry.notes: No register exists for physical format; it is a property of the offer.

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Grind is routinely modelled as a Shopify variant by specialty roasters, so many pages will expose it, while single-format sellers and supermarket-style listings will not name the state as an option at all. The wide band reflects that this is an untested split between two very different seller populations.

entries.consumer_note: If you own a grinder, whole bean is the format that keeps longest, because less surface area is exposed to oxygen. You can check this yourself by looking at whether the page lets you actually select whole bean, rather than at whether the word appears in the description.
entries.merchant_remediation: Expose the delivered physical state as a product option value with the words "Whole Bean", and make sure the corresponding variant is purchasable rather than permanently out of stock.

citations.source: EU Regulation 1169/2011, Annex VI Part A
citations.establishes: that the physical state or treatment of a food must form part of the name of the food where its omission could mislead, which is the legal basis for treating ground versus whole bean as a required disclosure rather than a preference

citations.source: National Coffee Association, storage and shelf life guidance
citations.establishes: that whole beans keep materially longer than ground coffee at room temperature because less surface area is exposed to oxygen, which is why the delivered state is a purchase-relevant fact and not a detail

binding.label: Whole bean option is listed and purchasable

adversarial.attack: A roaster lists a grind option literally named "Whole Bean or Ground — tell us in the order notes", which satisfies an option-value match while leaving the delivered state entirely undetermined at the point of purchase.
adversarial.resolution: The entry now states explicitly that an option naming several states, or deferring the choice to a free-text note, is not a purchasable whole-bean option. The engine cannot enforce that distinction, so it is recorded as residual risk rather than as a closed hole.
adversarial.residual_risk: The engine's variant match accepts an exact option-value match or a substring of the variant title, so any merchant-authored option value containing the phrase satisfies it. Option values are free text and this cannot be closed without a per-offer evidence model (ENGINE_GAPS G-12).

pass_means.establishes: That a purchasable option naming the whole-bean state exists on this product at the time of the test.
pass_means.does_not_establish: That whole beans are what a buyer receives by default, that the option is the one preselected, or that the coffee is unground at any point before dispatch.

known_gaps.corpus_case: no adversarial-corpus coverage exists for variant_option at all
known_gaps.note: The corpus covers materials, dimensions, care, claim and delivery. variant_option has no hostile cases, so its behaviour under merchant-authored option strings is unmeasured.

entries.question: Can I buy this already ground, so I do not need a grinder?

applicability.applies_when: the product is roasted coffee sold by mass rather than in pods or capsules
does_not_apply_when: pods, capsules and pre-dosed sachets, where the coffee is ground by definition

accepted_evidence.form: a purchasable option value naming the ground state
the matching variant is listed and marked available

insufficient_evidence.form: "freshly ground" or "ground to order"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A statement about when grinding happens is not a statement that a ground item is purchasable here, and some sellers use the phrase to describe what the buyer should do at home.

insufficient_evidence.form: "grind options available" in prose
insufficient_evidence.why_not: This announces that grinding exists as a service without making any ground item selectable, so a buyer cannot act on it at the point of purchase.

insufficient_evidence.form: a brew-method option name such as Espresso or Filter, treated as the generic ground state
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A named brew grind is a different, narrower assertion covered by its own entry, and a store may offer brew-specific grinds while offering no general ground option.

insufficient_evidence.form: the presence of a grind option list without any option being purchasable
insufficient_evidence.why_not: An option offered but permanently out of stock is not a format the buyer can receive, which the engine reports separately as listed and unavailable.

conflict_rules.when: the description says ground and only whole bean is purchasable
conflict_rules.resolution: the purchasable option list decides, because it is the offer

conflict_rules.when: both whole bean and ground are purchasable
conflict_rules.resolution: both this entry and the whole-bean entry pass independently; they are not mutually exclusive

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Specialty roasters who sell primarily whole bean often expose no general ground option, listing only brew-specific grinds or none at all, while mainstream sellers list ground as a first-class option. The split is genuinely unknown and the band is wide to say so.

entries.consumer_note: If you have no grinder, this is the question that decides whether the bag is usable to you. Check whether a ground option is actually selectable rather than whether the page mentions grinding, because many roasters describe a grinding service they do not offer as a purchasable option.
entries.merchant_remediation: Add a purchasable option value using the word "Ground" for the general pre-ground item, separately from any brew-specific grind names, and keep the variant in stock rather than describing the service in prose only.

citations.source: Independent refuting pass, live Google autocomplete retrieval (suggestqueries.google.com)
citations.establishes: that whole-bean versus ground is among the verified shopper-driven core coffee questions, ranked sixth of ten by the refuting pass on live search-intent evidence rather than on trade material

citations.source: National Coffee Association, storage and shelf life guidance
citations.establishes: that ground coffee holds one to two weeks at room temperature against one to three weeks for whole beans, so the delivered state changes the useful life of the purchase

citations.source: EU Regulation 1169/2011, Annex VI Part A
citations.establishes: that the physical state or treatment of a food forms part of the name of the food where omitting it could mislead, and the name of the food is a pre-purchase particular in distance selling under Article 14(1)(a)

refutation.challenged: Whether whole-bean-versus-ground is a shopper question or a trade preoccupation, and whether the EU name-of-food rule reaches a web page at all rather than only the physical pack.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass placed it in the verified shopper-driven core on live autocomplete evidence. The legal reading was narrowed: Article 14(1)(a) makes mandatory particulars available pre-purchase EXCEPT the durability date, so the name of the food does reach the page in the EU, while US net-quantity and organic labelling law reaches only the package. That distinction is applied throughout this standard.

binding.label: Ground option is listed and purchasable

adversarial.attack: A store offers a single option value named "Whole Bean — Ground on request at no charge", which contains the term, satisfies the engine's substring match against the variant title, and delivers whole beans unless the buyer separately emails.
adversarial.resolution: The entry states that an option combining several states, or making the ground state conditional on a request, is not a purchasable ground option. The engine's match cannot enforce this, so the limit is published rather than hidden.
adversarial.residual_risk: The engine accepts a substring of the variant title, so any merchant-authored option string containing "ground" passes — including unrelated words that contain the term. Closing this needs per-offer evidence resolution (ENGINE_GAPS G-12).

pass_means.establishes: That an option naming the ground state exists and is purchasable on this product at the time of the test.
pass_means.does_not_establish: That the coffee is ground fresh, ground at dispatch, ground to any particular size, or that ground is the state a buyer receives by default.

known_gaps.corpus_case: no adversarial-corpus coverage exists for variant_option at all
known_gaps.note: Behaviour under hostile merchant-authored option values is unmeasured for this requirement kind.

entries.question: Can I get this ground for espresso?

applicability.applies_when: the product is roasted coffee sold by mass and the seller offers any grind choice
does_not_apply_when: pods and capsules, where dose and grind are fixed by the format

accepted_evidence.form: a purchasable option value naming espresso as a grind
the matching variant is listed and marked available

insufficient_evidence.form: "Espresso Blend" or "Espresso Roast" as a product or blend name
insufficient_evidence.why_not: This is a naming and roast-style convention, not a grind claim; a whole-bean-only product can carry it, and treating the words as a grind assertion inverts what the seller said.

insufficient_evidence.form: "suitable for espresso" or "built for espresso" in prose
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A recommendation about which brewer the coffee suits is not an assertion that a matching grind is selectable, and it states nothing about particle size.

insufficient_evidence.form: a grind option named only by a number or grinder setting
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Grinder dial numbers are proprietary and are not comparable across grinders or even across units of the same model, so they name no point on any scale.

insufficient_evidence.form: "fine grind" offered as equivalent to espresso
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Fine, medium and coarse are seller-relative labels that published scales disagree about, and the espresso band alone spans roughly a factor of two, so a coarseness word does not resolve to the espresso case.

conflict_rules.when: the page recommends espresso brewing but offers no espresso grind option
conflict_rules.resolution: this entry fails; the brew-fit recommendation is a separate advisory question

conflict_rules.when: an espresso option exists but the page states a coarse micron figure
conflict_rules.resolution: record the internal contradiction rather than resolving it; the standard reports evidence, not which side is right

registry.notes: No body defines grind sizes, and no register of grind specifications exists.

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Espresso is the most commonly named brew-specific grind, but most sellers expose either no grind choice or only a general ground option, so the row should fail for a clear majority. The band sits high in the target range deliberately and the upper bound is set at the limit because a rate above it would carry little information.

entries.consumer_note: Grind size is the single thing most likely to make a good coffee taste bad in your brewer, and there is no agreed scale behind words like fine or medium. The check a buyer can do is whether the seller lets you pick a grind named for your machine, rather than trusting an adjective.
entries.merchant_remediation: Offer espresso as a named, purchasable grind option value rather than describing brewer suitability in prose, and state the particle-size target alongside it where you know it.

citations.source: Independent refuting pass, live Google autocomplete retrieval (suggestqueries.google.com)
citations.establishes: that five of the top ten autocomplete completions for "coffee grind" are brewer-specific and "coffee grind size chart" ranks first, making grind-to-brewer match the strongest verified shopper signal in the whole research corpus

citations.source: Specialty Coffee Association, coffee standards index
citations.establishes: that the trade's published standards cover sensory assessment, grinders and brewers but define no retail grind vocabulary, so a grind term on a bag resolves against no external definition

refutation.challenged: Whether brew-method grind fit is a real shopper question or a barista concern, given that the source material is largely roaster education.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass ranked it first of ten on live search-intent evidence and noted that no researcher had ranked it first. The scope was narrowed in response: this entry asserts only that a named grind option is purchasable, never that the grind is correct for the brewer, because no body defines the sizes.

binding.label: Espresso grind option is listed and purchasable

adversarial.attack: A roaster offers a single option value "Espresso" that denotes the blend style rather than a grind, on a product sold only as whole bean, so the row passes while no buyer can obtain an espresso grind.
adversarial.resolution: The entry names blend-style and roast-style uses of the word as insufficient, and its pass_means states that a pass does not establish a grind was applied. The engine cannot distinguish an option value's meaning, so the risk is disclosed.
adversarial.residual_risk: Where a seller uses "Espresso" as an option value for a roast style, the engine will pass and the standard has no mechanism to tell that apart from a grind option. This is the most likely false pass in this entry and it is not closed.

pass_means.establishes: That an option value naming espresso is purchasable on this product at the time of the test.
pass_means.does_not_establish: That the coffee is ground at all, that any particular particle size is delivered, or that the grind is suitable for the buyer's machine.

known_gaps.corpus_case: no adversarial-corpus coverage exists for variant_option at all

entries.question: Can I get this ground for a filter or pour-over brewer?

applicability.applies_when: the product is roasted coffee sold by mass and the seller offers any grind choice

accepted_evidence.form: a purchasable option value naming filter as a grind
the matching variant is listed and marked available

insufficient_evidence.form: "filter coffee" used as a category or serving style
insufficient_evidence.why_not: In much of the world the phrase names a beverage style rather than a grind, so its presence in prose asserts nothing about what is selectable.

insufficient_evidence.form: "suitable for all brew methods" or "one grind, every method"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The published grind bands for immersion and espresso do not overlap, so a single grind cannot suit every method; this is the most confidently wrong claim in the class and a naive check accepts it because it is maximally inclusive.

insufficient_evidence.form: a brewing-guides navigation block listing pour-over, drip and AeroPress
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Site navigation and topic lists are chrome rather than an assertion about this item, and the engine deliberately excludes raw page text from evidence for exactly this reason.

insufficient_evidence.form: "medium grind" offered as equivalent to filter
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Coarseness words are seller-relative and two published scales disagree about where medium sits, so the word does not resolve to the filter case.

conflict_rules.when: the page names pour-over in prose but offers only whole bean
conflict_rules.resolution: this entry fails; a recommendation is not a purchasable option

conflict_rules.when: both Filter and Espresso options exist
conflict_rules.resolution: both entries pass independently; they describe different offers on the same product

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Filter is named less consistently than espresso and competes with pour-over, drip and V60 as option wording, so the fixed string will miss stores that offer the same thing under a different name. The high band reflects vocabulary fragmentation as much as seller behaviour, and that is a weakness of the assertion rather than a finding about merchants.

entries.consumer_note: If you brew with a cone, a Chemex or a drip machine, this is the grind you need, and the words sellers use for it vary. Look for a selectable option rather than a sentence, and treat any claim that one grind suits every brewer as unreliable.
entries.merchant_remediation: Name the filter or pour-over grind as a purchasable option value, and avoid offering a single grind described as suitable for all methods, which cannot be true across immersion and espresso.

citations.source: Independent refuting pass, live Google autocomplete retrieval (suggestqueries.google.com)
citations.establishes: that brewer-specific grind queries dominate the coffee-grind autocomplete set, including pour over, french press, moka pot, cold brew and percolator, which is direct current search-intent evidence rather than trade material

citations.source: Specialty Coffee Association, coffee standards index
citations.establishes: that no published trade standard defines retail grind designations, so a filter grind claim is checkable only as a stated designation and never as a measured particle size

refutation.challenged: Whether a single fixed option string can represent a question whose vocabulary is fragmented across filter, pour-over, drip and V60.
refutation.resolution: It cannot, and the entry now says so in its own discrimination reasoning: a failure may mean the seller uses different wording rather than that no filter grind exists. The general form of this question needs an enumerated-value matcher and is published separately as blocked under ENGINE_GAPS G-03.

binding.label: Filter grind option is listed and purchasable

adversarial.attack: A store names its bag-size options "Filter Pack 250g" and "Filter Pack 1kg", where Filter is part of a pack name rather than a grind, so every size satisfies the assertion while the coffee ships whole bean.
adversarial.resolution: The entry records pack-name and category uses of the word as insufficient, and pass_means limits what a pass establishes to the existence of the option value. The engine cannot read the option's intent, so the risk is stated.
adversarial.residual_risk: Any merchant-authored option value containing "filter" passes, including pack names and category words. The inverse error is larger in practice: sellers who offer this grind under another name fail, which makes the predicted band partly a measurement of vocabulary rather than of merchants.

pass_means.establishes: That an option value naming filter is purchasable on this product at the time of the test.
pass_means.does_not_establish: That a particular particle size is delivered, that it suits the buyer's brewer, or that the option means a grind rather than a pack or a category.

known_gaps.corpus_case: no adversarial-corpus coverage exists for variant_option at all

entries.question: How much coffee do I get — is there a weight anywhere on this page?

applicability.applies_when: the product is coffee sold by mass, including pod packs that also declare a net weight

accepted_evidence.form: a number bound to a unit of mass in a readable sentence
accepted_evidence.example: 12 oz bag of whole bean coffee.

accepted_evidence.form: a number bound to a unit of mass in the product title
a mass measurement inside the JSON-LD product description prose

insufficient_evidence.form: a size option named Small, Medium, Large, Bag or Standard
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A size label with no unit states no quantity, and a buyer cannot compare two sellers or compute a unit price from it.

insufficient_evidence.form: a brew ratio or dose in grams, such as "use 18 g per 300 ml"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: This is a usage quantity measured inside the product rather than a measurement of the product, and the engine currently credits it — a pinned corpus defect this entry inherits in the false-pass direction.

insufficient_evidence.form: a shipping or dispatch weight
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It includes packaging and is systematically higher than the net quantity, and it is often the only number a machine can find on a fulfilment-heavy page.

insufficient_evidence.form: a pod or capsule count with no mass
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Dose per capsule ranges from roughly five to thirteen grams across systems, so a count is not convertible to a coffee mass.

insufficient_evidence.form: a brewed-yield volume such as "makes 2 litres of concentrate"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Yield is a use statement at an undisclosed dilution, not a declaration of how much coffee is in the package.

insufficient_evidence.form: a weight visible only in a product photograph
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Image content is not page text, is not read by the engine, and product photography frequently shows a different size or an older bag design.

conflict_rules.when: the title states one mass and the page sells several sizes
conflict_rules.resolution: record that a mass is stated and that it cannot be attributed to a specific offer; do not report it as the net quantity of the purchase

conflict_rules.when: a mass appears only in a specification block the engine cannot quote
conflict_rules.resolution: the row passes and names the surface without a quote, which the engine already reports honestly

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Coffee titles very commonly carry a mass, and the product title is a quotable evidence surface, so this row should pass on a clear majority of pages. The band sits at the bottom of the target range and the entry is worth running mainly because a coffee page with no mass anywhere is a genuine, actionable defect for a machine buyer.

entries.consumer_note: A price is uninterpretable without a weight: an eighteen-dollar bag could be ten ounces or twelve, a twenty per cent difference invisible to any comparison. If the page shows no mass, you cannot work out what you are paying per cup.
entries.merchant_remediation: State the net quantity in a readable sentence on the product page and per purchasable size, in both metric and the customary unit for your market, rather than relying on the title alone when several sizes share one page.

citations.source: EU Regulation 1169/2011, Article 9(1)(e) and Article 14(1)(a)
citations.establishes: that net quantity is a mandatory particular and that in distance selling every mandatory particular except the durability date must be available before the purchase is concluded, which makes net quantity a pre-purchase page duty in the EU specifically

citations.source: US FDA, 21 CFR 101.7 net quantity of contents
citations.establishes: that the US declaration duty attaches to the principal display panel of a food in package form and says nothing about internet listings, so US net-quantity law is a package rule and not a page rule

citations.source: Independent refuting pass, live Google autocomplete retrieval (suggestqueries.google.com)
citations.establishes: that cost transparency including net weight and unit price sits in the verified shopper-driven core, ranked seventh of ten on live search-intent evidence

refutation.challenged: The research labelled net quantity flatly mandated while citing US package-labelling law as authority for a web page.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass identified this as the dominant defect across the whole corpus: 21 CFR 101.7 contains no reference to internet or online listings, so US law does not mandate a weight on a page. Only the EU distance-selling route makes it a pre-purchase duty. The citation set and the demand basis were rewritten accordingly, and the assertion is deliberately worded as "a mass measurement is stated" rather than as a compliance claim.

binding.label: A weight or measurement is stated in readable text

adversarial.attack: A page whose only mass anywhere is a brewing instruction — "We recommend 60 g of coffee per litre of water" — passes as having stated a measurement, and the merchant is told their measurements are published when the net quantity of the bag appears nowhere.
adversarial.resolution: The brew-ratio and usage-quantity forms are named as insufficient, the entry declares the pinned corpus defect that makes them pass today, and pass_means restricts the conclusion to "a mass appears on a product surface" rather than "the net quantity is published".
adversarial.residual_risk: Until the pinned usage-quantity defect is closed, a page stating only a brew ratio or a nutrition quantity satisfies this assertion. The label was chosen to be true even in that case, which limits the damage without removing it.

pass_means.establishes: That a number bound to a unit of mass appears in readable product text on a surface the engine may quote.
pass_means.does_not_establish: That the value is the net quantity of the package, that it applies to the option the buyer selected, or that it is anything other than a dose, a yield or a dispatch weight.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "Each serving contains 12 grams of protein."
known_gaps.note: A quantity measured inside the product reads as a measurement of the product. Found on a real store during the v2.8 fitness run and being fixed concurrently; the coffee analogue is a brew ratio in grams.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "Steep in 8 oz of hot water for 3 minutes."
known_gaps.note: A usage instruction quantity. Directly analogous to brewing guidance on a coffee page.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "Minimum order 5 kg." and "Discount applies to purchases over 10 lbs."
known_gaps.note: Order thresholds read as product measurements. Wholesale coffee pages carry these routinely.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "Weighs 3 lbs and ships free."
known_gaps.note: A genuine weight vetoed because the sentence also mentions shipping. Coffee pages often combine weight and free-shipping wording in one sentence.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "This mug holds 12 fl. oz."
known_gaps.note: Abbreviated units are split across sentence fragments by the tokenizer. Coffee weights are frequently written "12 fl. oz." and "1 lb."

entries.question: Does this page say the coffee is organic?

applicability.applies_when: the product is roasted coffee offered to consumers in any format

accepted_evidence.form: an explicit organic statement naming the certifying agent
the same statement inside the JSON-LD product description
the same statement in FAQ structured data

insufficient_evidence.form: the bare word "organic"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: An operation selling under the US small-operation threshold may lawfully call its product organic without certification, so the word alone is evidence of nothing checkable.

insufficient_evidence.form: "organically grown", "organic practices", "beyond organic", "transitional"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: None of these sits inside the four regulated label tiers, and "beyond organic" specifically is marketing that positions itself as superior to the only checkable category.

insufficient_evidence.form: "made with organic ingredients"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: That is a distinct and lower labelling tier with a seventy per cent threshold which may not use the seal, and a naive check scores it as equivalent to organic.

insufficient_evidence.form: a rendered organic seal image with no agent named
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Image content is not page text and the seal resolves to nothing on its own; the certifier's name is the field the rule requires precisely because the seal is unverifiable without it.

insufficient_evidence.form: a farm's or exporter's certificate offered while the roaster is uncertified
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Only a certified handler may use the seal, so the register must resolve to the roaster; this is the most legitimate-looking substitution in coffee because the farm genuinely is certified.

insufficient_evidence.form: an EU control-body code such as XX-BIO-NNN treated as identifying the seller
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The code identifies the control body that audits, never the operator audited, so a check that resolves the code has verified nothing about this seller.

insufficient_evidence.form: "certified organic since 2011"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A certification history is not a current status, and the register publishes surrendered, suspended and revoked precisely because real certificates stop being real.

conflict_rules.when: the description claims organic and the shipping policy page also contains the word
conflict_rules.resolution: read only product surfaces; a document about orders is not evidence about this product

conflict_rules.when: an organic claim and a contradicting statement both appear
conflict_rules.resolution: the engine reports the contradiction and does not pass the row, which is the correct fail-closed behaviour

registry.register_name: USDA National Organic Program — Organic INTEGRITY Database
registry.lookup_key: the certified operation's legal name, client ID or certificate number
registry.lookup_method: Search the database by operation name, certifying agent, certified product, client ID or certificate number; the record carries a status of Certified, Surrendered, Suspended or Revoked, the certifier, and the certified-product scope, and the certificate itself can be downloaded. Bulk spreadsheet exports and monthly full-dataset snapshots were confirmed live by an independent verification pass; the documented REST API was not — its developer help page returns an application error.
registry.notes: The engine has no register client, so this entry adjudicates only the on-page statement. The resolution step is published separately as a blocked entry.

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Organic is common in specialty coffee but far from universal, and the engine's dictionary matches the bare word as well as the certified phrasings, so the row will pass wherever the word appears at all. The band is wide because the pass condition is looser than the question a buyer is asking.

entries.consumer_note: The word organic on its own can be lawful without any certification for a small seller, so what matters is whether a certifying agent is named. You can check a named agent and the roaster's legal name against the USDA Organic INTEGRITY Database yourself, free, and see whether the certificate is current.
entries.merchant_remediation: If a certifying agent certified the operation that packs this coffee, name that agent in product-page text alongside the legal operation name, so a reader can resolve the pair in the public register rather than taking a seal image on trust.

citations.source: US National Organic Program, 7 CFR 205.303
citations.establishes: that where a packaged product is labelled organic the certifying agent's name must appear on the information panel, which is why a named agent rather than a seal is the evidence a reader needs

citations.source: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service, published organic enforcement settlements
citations.establishes: that organic misrepresentation is a real and enforced failure mode in coffee specifically, including a roaster that settled for a fifteen-thousand-dollar civil penalty for representing products as organic without certification

citations.source: CCOF, guidance on using the Organic INTEGRITY Database
citations.establishes: that the register is described by a certifying agent authorised under the national organic programme as the official place to check whether an operation is certified, which is the intended verification route rather than the agent's own word

refutation.challenged: Whether the claim is mandated on a product page, and whether shoppers actually verify certificates rather than simply preferring certified products.
refutation.resolution: Both challenges landed. The labelling rule is titled for packaged products and places the agent's name on the information panel, so it does not reach a web page — the status here is voluntary disclosure, not a page mandate. And the refuting pass established that certificate auditing is importer and retail-buyer behaviour, not shopper behaviour, which is why this entry adjudicates only whether a claim is stated and the register-resolution question is published as blocked with trade rather than shopper grounding.

binding.label: An organic claim is stated in readable text

adversarial.attack: A page reading "We follow organic farming principles on every lot we buy" passes the assertion, because the engine's dictionary matches the bare word, while the seller holds no certification and has carefully avoided claiming any.
adversarial.resolution: The practice-language forms are named as insufficient and pass_means states plainly that a pass does not establish certification. The engine's claim dictionary is closed and cannot be narrowed from a standard, so the limit is published rather than fixed.
adversarial.residual_risk: Any sentence containing the word organic passes, including hedged practice language and a statement about the packaging being organic cotton. This is the widest gap between what the assertion tests and what the question asks, and closing it needs a certifier-name matcher (ENGINE_GAPS G-06).

pass_means.establishes: That readable product text on this page states an organic claim of some form, quoted verbatim where a clean sentence exists.
pass_means.does_not_establish: That any operation is certified, that a certifying agent was named, that the claim resolves in any register, or that the claim is about the coffee rather than the packaging.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "A gift bundle of our house blends." with an organic phrase in the shipping policy's page title
known_gaps.note: Claim rows do not exclude the shipping-policy surface and the policy fold-in carries SEO chrome, so a claim about the product can be proven from a document about orders. Found on a real tea store and being fixed concurrently.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "Love that it's fragrance-free!" — a customer in Portland.
known_gaps.note: A review quote credited as the store's own statement. Applies to every claim row, and coffee pages carry heavy review content.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "The tube is BPA-free."
known_gaps.note: A container property credited to the contents. The coffee analogue is an organic-cotton or compostable-bag claim crediting the coffee.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "Most cheap versions are made from thin stamped steel."
known_gaps.note: The comparative veto tolerates only one word between "most" and its verb, so "Most supermarket blends are organic" would credit a competitor's property to this product.

entries.question: Does this page say the coffee is fair trade?

applicability.applies_when: the product is roasted coffee offered to consumers in any format

accepted_evidence.form: an explicit scheme claim naming the certified counterparty
accepted_evidence.example: Fairtrade certified beans from a co-operative in Huila.

accepted_evidence.form: the same statement inside the JSON-LD product description
the same statement in FAQ structured data

insufficient_evidence.form: lowercase generic "fair trade", "fairly traded", "fair trade principles"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: These sit outside every scheme, and their lexical closeness to the certified mark is the whole problem: a reader cannot tell a scheme claim from a sentiment.

insufficient_evidence.form: "we believe fair trade should be the industry standard"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: An aspiration about the industry is not a claim about this product, and the engine currently credits it — a pinned corpus defect that makes this the least reliable executable entry in the standard.

insufficient_evidence.form: a Fair Trade USA seal treated as the same thing as the FAIRTRADE Mark
insufficient_evidence.why_not: They are different schemes with different standards, different marks and different registers, and one of the two registers is behind a login, so conflating them launders the unverifiable one.

insufficient_evidence.form: a co-operative's certification identifier presented as the roaster's
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The co-operative's certification is genuine and the inference is wrong; the mark on a consumer pack requires a licence held by the brand, which is a separate arrangement.

insufficient_evidence.form: a rendered scheme logo with no identifier
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A logo image is not page text, resolves to nothing, and is the easiest element on a page to copy.

insufficient_evidence.form: "we pay above the market price" or "direct trade"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: These are real trade practices with no scheme, no definition and no register, so they are self-declared and are routinely substituted for a scheme claim.

insufficient_evidence.form: a mass-balance or sourcing-programme variant read as product certification
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A certificate-holder record cannot establish what fraction of the coffee in a given bag is certified, so a sourcing-programme claim answers a different question.

conflict_rules.when: a scheme claim appears only in a review quote or a customer question
conflict_rules.resolution: a customer's words are not the store's statement and must not satisfy the assertion

conflict_rules.when: two different schemes are named on one page
conflict_rules.resolution: record both as stated; the standard does not rank schemes or resolve which applies to this lot

registry.operator: FLOCERT, the Fairtrade International certification body
registry.lookup_key: a FLO ID or the certified organisation's exact legal name
registry.lookup_method: A free public search browsable by certification status, product, country, function or keyword. Confirmed live and free by an independent verification pass, with the full certified-customer list behind a login. No public API or bulk download. Note that Fair Trade USA, a different scheme, has no free public certificate lookup at all — its authoritative search is behind a partner-portal login, confirmed directly.
registry.notes: Consumer packs and product pages essentially never publish a FLO ID, so even with a register the claim is detect-only in practice.

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Scheme claims are less common than organic in specialty coffee, where direct-trade language often replaces them, but the engine's dictionary also matches the generic lowercase phrase, so the pass condition is much broader than the scheme question. The band reflects both effects pulling in opposite directions.

entries.consumer_note: There are several different fair-trade schemes and one generic phrase that belongs to none of them, so the useful question is which scheme is named and who is certified under it. One of the two main schemes publishes a free searchable register; the other keeps its authoritative lookup behind a login, so a claim under it cannot be checked from outside.
entries.merchant_remediation: Name the scheme exactly, name the certified counterparty, and publish the scheme identifier where you hold one, so that a reader can resolve the claim in the scheme's own register instead of relying on a logo.

citations.source: Fairtrade International, traceability in Fairtrade supply chains
citations.establishes: that all Fairtrade coffee is fully physically traceable while cocoa, tea, sugar and juices may use mass balance, and that certified producers and traders are distinct from licensees who put the mark on a consumer pack

citations.source: FLOCERT Fairtrade Customer Search
citations.establishes: that a free public search of certified organisations exists and is browsable by status, product, country and function, confirmed live by an independent verification pass

citations.source: Fair Trade USA Partner Portal search
citations.establishes: that the authoritative status lookup for the other main scheme renders a login screen, confirmed by direct fetch, so a claim under it cannot be resolved by any outside reader or automated check

refutation.challenged: Whether shoppers ask this at all, and whether treating two different schemes as one interchangeable claim is defensible.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass confirmed shoppers do buy certified coffee and search for what fair trade means, while certificate auditing is trade behaviour. It also found that treating the two schemes as one silently downgrades the verifiable scheme and launders the unverifiable one. The entry now separates the schemes explicitly in its evidence rules and registry block, and its pass_means refuses any scheme conclusion.

binding.label: A fair-trade scheme claim is stated in readable text

adversarial.attack: A page reading "We believe fair trade should be the industry standard, and we are working toward it" passes the assertion today, so a seller who has explicitly told the buyer it is NOT certified is recorded as having stated the claim.
adversarial.resolution: This attack succeeds against the engine, not merely against the wording: it is a pinned corpus defect. The entry names the aspiration form as insufficient, declares the corpus case in known_gaps, and states in pass_means that a pass establishes only that matching text exists. This is the entry a reader should trust least.
adversarial.residual_risk: Until the pinned aspiration defect is closed, an explicit denial of certification satisfies this assertion. That is the worst residual risk in the standard and it is the reason this entry's pass_means is worded more defensively than any other.

pass_means.establishes: That readable product text on this page contains a fair-trade phrase of some form, quoted verbatim where a clean sentence exists.
pass_means.does_not_establish: That any scheme certified anyone, which scheme is meant, that the seller holds a licence, or that the phrase is a claim rather than an aspiration or a comparison.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "We believe fair trade should be the industry standard."
known_gaps.note: The single most damaging collision in this standard: an aspiration, and in context often a denial, is credited as a stated claim. Pinned open in the corpus.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "Love that it's fragrance-free!" — a customer in Portland.
known_gaps.note: Review quotes credited as the store's statement, which applies to every claim row.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "A gift bundle of our house blends." with the claim phrase in shipping-policy chrome
known_gaps.note: Claim rows accept the shipping-policy surface; being fixed concurrently.

entries.question: Is this coffee from one place, or is it a blend?

applicability.applies_when: the product is roasted coffee offered to consumers in any format

accepted_evidence.form: an explicit single-origin claim with a named place at region level or finer
accepted_evidence.example: Single origin from one farm in Huila, Colombia.

accepted_evidence.form: the same statement inside the JSON-LD product description
the claim in the product title where the title also names the place

insufficient_evidence.form: "single origin: Ethiopia" or any country-only claim
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A country with dozens of non-comparable growing zones is true and uninformative; the minimum non-misleading content is a place specific enough that a buyer could ask about it.

insufficient_evidence.form: "100% Colombian"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A national blend of thousands of farms satisfies this exactly; it is a purity claim about a country, not a claim about granularity.

insufficient_evidence.form: a single-origin claim on a page that names two or more regions
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The label and the content contradict each other, and a keyword check passes it because the phrase is present.

insufficient_evidence.form: "direct trade", "relationship coffee", "farm direct"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: These are sourcing-relationship claims routinely substituted for granularity claims, and they say nothing about how many places the coffee came from.

insufficient_evidence.form: "single farm" where the named entity is a washing station
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A station buying cherry from hundreds of smallholders is one site rather than one farm, so the words overstate the granularity by an order of magnitude.

insufficient_evidence.form: "our single origin range" or a collection-level statement
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A statement about the seller's catalogue is not a statement about this product, and the engine cannot tell the two apart.

conflict_rules.when: the title says single origin and the description names a blend of countries
conflict_rules.resolution: record the contradiction; the standard reports that the page disagrees with itself rather than choosing a side

conflict_rules.when: the seller publishes its own definition of single origin elsewhere on the site
conflict_rules.resolution: a site-level definition does not change what this page states; evidence is read from product surfaces only

registry.notes: No body defines single origin, and no register records origin granularity for a retail lot.

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Blends are at least as common as single-origin lots in retail coffee, and blends will correctly fail, but the engine's dictionary also matches "single estate" and "single farm" and will pass any sentence containing them regardless of subject. The band is wide because the pass condition is looser than the question.

entries.consumer_note: Single origin has no agreed definition, so it can mean one farm or one country, and those are very different purchases. The useful check is whether a place is named at region level or finer, because a country name alone tells you almost nothing about what is in the bag.
entries.merchant_remediation: State the granularity and the named entity at that level — region and municipality for a regional lot, the farm or estate name for a single-farm lot, or the co-operative and the number of contributing producers for an aggregated lot — rather than the phrase alone.

citations.source: Coffee & Conservation, independent coffee certification and sourcing reference
citations.establishes: that long-running independent consumer reference material exists to explain what coffee sourcing and certification labels do and do not mean, which is written because shoppers cannot read the labels unaided

citations.source: ISO 3509 coffee and coffee products vocabulary, as summarised in trade reference material
citations.establishes: that the international coffee vocabulary defines processing classes but contains no definition of single origin, single estate or microlot, so those terms resolve against no external definition

refutation.challenged: Whether single-origin granularity is a shopper question or a specialty-trade preoccupation, given that the supporting sources mostly define terms.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass placed the specialty-provenance tier as largely trade-invented and cited only glossaries and importer guides for it, warning that a source defining a term is not evidence anyone asks. The narrower shopper question — one place or a blend — survives, so this entry was kept while the finer provenance questions (variety, elevation, lot identity, origin grade, cupping score) were demoted to advisory or dropped and recorded in GROUNDING.md.

binding.label: A single-origin claim is stated in readable text

adversarial.attack: A blend page reading "Unlike our single origin lots, this blend is built for milk" passes the assertion, because the phrase is present and the comparative veto tolerates only one word between the contrast marker and its verb — so a sentence whose whole purpose is to say this is NOT single origin is credited as stating that it is.
adversarial.resolution: Collection-level and comparative uses are named as insufficient and the shared comparative-veto defect is declared in known_gaps. The engine's claim dictionary cannot be narrowed from a standard, so the limit is published.
adversarial.residual_risk: Any sentence containing the phrase passes, including one that contrasts this product against the seller's single-origin range. The inverse also holds: a genuine single-origin lot that names only a farm without using the phrase fails.

pass_means.establishes: That readable product text on this page contains a single-origin phrase, quoted verbatim where a clean sentence exists.
pass_means.does_not_establish: The granularity of the origin, that a place is named at all, that the claim is not contradicted elsewhere on the page, or that the sentence is about this product rather than the seller's range.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "Most cheap versions are made from thin stamped steel."
known_gaps.note: The comparative veto in subject.ts tolerates exactly one word between "most" and its verb, so two-word noun phrases walk through. The coffee analogue credits a contrast against the seller's own other products.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "Love that it's fragrance-free!" — a customer in Portland.
known_gaps.note: Review quotes credited as the store's statement.

entries.question: Can a shopping assistant match this exact bag to a catalogue entry?

applicability.applies_when: the product page publishes readable Product structured data
does_not_apply_when: the page markup could not be read, which the engine reports as requiring store access rather than as an absence
applicability.signal: presence of a JSON-LD Product node

accepted_evidence.form: a GTIN in JSON-LD whose check digit validates after separators are stripped, or an MPN that is not a placeholder

insufficient_evidence.form: a placeholder value such as N/A, TBD, PLACEHOLDER or YOUR-MPN-HERE, in any punctuated or suffixed form
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A merchant filling a required field with nothing is how these values arise, and a value that identifies nothing cannot do the job the row promises.

insufficient_evidence.form: an all-zero GTIN
insufficient_evidence.why_not: All zeros satisfies the check-digit arithmetic and identifies no product, so the arithmetic alone is not a sufficient test.

insufficient_evidence.form: a value with the right length and a wrong check digit
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A mistyped or invented identifier resolves to nothing in any catalogue, so length is not evidence of validity.

insufficient_evidence.form: an internal SKU published in the GTIN field
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A seller-private stock code is not a global identifier and cannot match this product to any external catalogue entry.

insufficient_evidence.form: an identifier stated in prose rather than in structured data
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The engine reads identifiers only from structured data, and prose identifiers are not machine-consumable in the way a shopping assistant needs.

conflict_rules.when: the GTIN is invalid but a real MPN is present
conflict_rules.resolution: the row passes on the MPN alone, and the engine names which identifier it read

conflict_rules.when: different variants carry different barcodes
conflict_rules.resolution: the engine reads the product-level node only; per-variant identity is a known limitation published as a blocked entry

registry.notes: A GTIN is allocated under a global numbering system, but no free public register resolves an arbitrary GTIN to a product record, so the engine validates form rather than resolving identity.

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Small roasters overwhelmingly sell without barcodes and Shopify does not require one, so most coffee pages should fail, while packaged-goods sellers reaching grocery channels will have them. The band is high and the upper bound is set at the target limit because a rate above it would carry little information.

entries.consumer_note: This is the field that lets an assistant tell your bag apart from a similarly-named one, and it is why searching by product name sometimes surfaces the wrong seller. You can look for it yourself in the page source, though most small roasters publish none.
entries.merchant_remediation: Publish a valid GTIN or a real manufacturer part number in the Product structured data, and never fill the field with a placeholder, because an unusable value is worse than an absent one for a machine consumer.

citations.source: Google Merchant Center product data specification
citations.establishes: that the dominant product-feed specification treats a global trade item number as the field that identifies a product to an automated consumer, which is what makes its absence a machine-buying defect rather than a cosmetic one

citations.source: GS1 general specifications overview
citations.establishes: that a global trade item number is allocated under a defined numbering system with a computed check digit, which is the basis for validating a published value rather than accepting any digit string

refutation.challenged: Whether shoppers ask this at all, since a buyer does not read structured data.
refutation.resolution: Shoppers do not ask it in these words, and the entry no longer claims they do — its demand basis is machine-consumer convention rather than buyer community evidence. It is retained because the whole premise of the product is that assistants read these pages, and because the assertion is structural and cheap to check. Its consumer_note is written to explain the consequence a shopper does experience.

binding.label: A product identifier is published in structured data

adversarial.attack: A seller publishes the same valid GTIN across every size and grind of a coffee, so the identifier validates, the row passes, and an assistant matching on it retrieves the wrong bag every time except one.
adversarial.resolution: No change was made, because the assertion is deliberately about publication rather than uniqueness and its pass_means already refuses the identity conclusion.
adversarial.residual_risk: A syntactically valid identifier that is duplicated across variants, or that belongs to a different product entirely, passes this assertion. The engine validates form and cannot resolve identity, and no free public register would let it, so this cannot be closed by any change to the standard.

pass_means.establishes: That the page publishes a structurally plausible product identifier that is not a placeholder and, for a GTIN, has a valid check digit.
pass_means.does_not_establish: That the identifier is correct, unique to this product, allocated to this seller, or resolvable to any catalogue record anywhere.

entries.notes: This entry passes publicly and regresses the moment a merchant connects their store: the authenticated snapshot sets the page-markup field to null, so the row returns requires_store_access for a store we have access to, while the barcode sits in the synced catalog. Recorded as ENGINE_GAPS G-07.

entries.question: When will this actually be sent to me?

applicability.applies_when: the product is physically shipped to the buyer

accepted_evidence.form: a stated dispatch or delivery window with a number and a unit
the same statement in FAQ structured data
the same statement in the publicly readable shipping policy

insufficient_evidence.form: "free shipping" or a shipping price
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Price is not speed, and crediting it was the live false positive that caused the engine's entire evidence-validation layer to be written.

insufficient_evidence.form: "fast shipping", "ships fast", "quick dispatch"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: An adjective with no number and no unit states no window a buyer or a machine can act on.

insufficient_evidence.form: a returns window such as "returns accepted within 30 business days"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A returns period answers a different question, and the engine currently credits it as a delivery window — a pinned corpus defect this entry inherits.

insufficient_evidence.form: "roasted to order" or "always freshly roasted"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: These describe the workflow rather than the latency and are compatible with a single weekly roast day that adds days before dispatch.

insufficient_evidence.form: a transit estimate such as "delivered in 3-5 days" with no handling time
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Transit alone omits the handling component, which is the part that varies most between roasters and the part a roast-to-order operation controls.

insufficient_evidence.form: a delivery estimate shown only in the cart or after a postcode is entered
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It is not on the product page, so a pre-purchase reader and an automated check cannot see it.

conflict_rules.when: the product page and the shipping policy state different windows
conflict_rules.resolution: the engine reports the first supporting sentence it finds and names its surface; the standard records that the page disagrees with the policy

conflict_rules.when: the shipping policy could not be read
conflict_rules.resolution: report that the surface was not inspectable rather than that no window is published — the difference between a finding and an accusation

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: The engine has measured this row failing for about seventy-one per cent of stores in a general sample, which sits inside this band; coffee may differ in either direction because roast-to-order sellers discuss timing more than average while also being the least likely to commit to a number. The band is anchored on a real measurement of a different population, which is the strongest basis any prediction in this standard has.

entries.consumer_note: For coffee the handling time matters more than the courier, because a bag can sit for days waiting for the next roast. Look for a stated dispatch window with a number in it, and treat a transit estimate or a free-shipping badge as answering a different question.
entries.merchant_remediation: State a dispatch window with a number and a unit on the product page or in the shipping policy, for example that orders ship within two business days, and state it separately from courier transit time.

citations.source: EU Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU, Article 6(1)
citations.establishes: that for a distance contract the trader must give the time by which it undertakes to deliver the goods before the consumer is bound, which is a genuine pre-contract web-page duty rather than a package-labelling rule

citations.source: US FTC Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule, 16 CFR 435.2
citations.establishes: that a seller must have a reasonable basis for a stated shipment time and must ship within thirty days where no time is stated, which makes the stated window a regulated representation in advertising rather than an optional courtesy

citations.source: Internal measurement recorded in src/server/productTest.ts
citations.establishes: that this requirement failed for about seventy-one per cent of stores in the engine's own production sample, which is the only measured discrimination figure available to anchor a prediction in this standard

refutation.challenged: Whether the commercial-terms mandates cited here are genuine web-page duties or, like the food-labelling rules, package-only obligations borrowed to lend authority.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass drew this distinction explicitly and found the commercial-terms instruments — the Consumer Rights Directive, the FTC order rule, price-indication and negative-option rules — genuinely are web-page and advertising obligations, in contrast to the food-labelling rules it corrected elsewhere in this standard.

binding.label: A dispatch or delivery window is stated

adversarial.attack: A shipping policy reading "Returns are accepted within 30 business days of receipt" passes the assertion, so a store that publishes no delivery window at all is recorded as having stated one, quoting its returns policy as the proof.
adversarial.resolution: The returns-window form is named as insufficient and the pinned corpus case is declared. The engine's timing vocabulary is closed and cannot be narrowed from a standard, so the defect is published rather than fixed.
adversarial.residual_risk: Any sentence containing a business-days phrase and a digit may satisfy this row regardless of subject, and negation coordination across a comma also defeats the denial guard, so an explicit refusal to commit to a window can pass.

pass_means.establishes: That readable text on a product surface or the public shipping policy states a dispatch or delivery interval with a number.
pass_means.does_not_establish: That the interval is honoured, that it covers handling as well as transit, that it applies to this product rather than to orders generally, or that the interval is about delivery rather than returns.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "Returns are accepted within 30 business days of receipt."
known_gaps.note: A returns window credited as a delivery window. Pinned open, and coffee shipping policies routinely place both in the same document.

known_gaps.corpus_case: "We do not offer weekend pickup, or overnight shipping."
known_gaps.note: Negation does not reach past the comma, so the second conjunct of a denial reads as a stated delivery speed.

known_gaps.corpus_case: a denial, then a colon, then a delivery window — the ordinary FAQ and spec-label shape
known_gaps.note: A colon is an unconditional clause boundary, so any colon between the negator and the term resets the clause and the denial reads as a stated delivery speed. The corpus records this case with the assurance verb the claim linter forbids, which is why it is described here rather than quoted.

entries.notes: This is one of two requirement kinds that pass evidence to the matcher without first filtering sentences the claim linter would refuse, so a shipping policy containing the linter's forbidden assurance word can return the merchant's ENTIRE report as unreachable. Coffee raises the odds because freshness and delivery assurance language is central to the category. Recorded as ENGINE_GAPS G-08.

entries.question: What does this cost?

applicability.applies_when: any purchasable coffee product

accepted_evidence.form: a readable variant price, which the platform exposes on essentially every product

insufficient_evidence.form: a price with no net weight beside it
insufficient_evidence.why_not: An eighteen-dollar bag could be ten ounces or twelve, a twenty per cent difference invisible to any comparison, so a bare price does not answer what the coffee costs.

insufficient_evidence.form: a strikethrough or reference price
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A price the seller never charged is a comparison device rather than the cost of this purchase, and price-indication rules target exactly that.

insufficient_evidence.form: a headline price that is the subscription rate
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Where a recurring option is preselected and cheaper, the most prominent number on the page is a recurring commitment rather than the one-off cost.

conflict_rules.when: several variants carry different prices
conflict_rules.resolution: the engine reads the lowest readable price across variants, which is not the price of any particular offer

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: The engine has measured a price requirement failing for zero of thirteen stores, because a price is exposed on essentially every platform product. A row that passes for everyone carries exactly as little information as one that fails for everyone, so this question is published and deliberately not run. It is the canonical zero-information assertion and the reason this tier exists.

entries.consumer_note: The price is always the easiest thing to find on a coffee page and almost never the thing that is missing. What is frequently missing is the weight beside it, which is what makes the price mean something, and that is asked separately.
entries.merchant_remediation: Nothing to remediate: the platform exposes a price on every product. The useful work is stating the net quantity for each purchasable size so the price can be compared.

citations.source: EU Directive 98/6/EC on the indication of prices
citations.establishes: that the selling price and, for products sold by mass, the unit price must both be indicated to consumers, which is why the interesting assertion in this class is the unit price rather than the price

citations.source: Internal measurement recorded in src/server/productTest.ts
citations.establishes: that a price requirement failed for zero of thirteen real stores in the engine's own sample and was documented as carrying the same amount of information as one that failed for all thirteen, namely none

refutation.challenged: Whether omitting price entirely would look like an oversight in a published standard.
refutation.resolution: It would, which is why the question is published with its measured zero failure rate rather than dropped. This entry is one of the two cases that forced a fourth tier into the grammar, because the three original tiers could only describe it as untestable, which is false, or as executable, which would be noise.

entries.question: Can I actually buy this right now?

applicability.applies_when: any coffee product page a buyer can reach
applicability.signal: availability data in structured data or the variant list

accepted_evidence.form: at least one variant listed as available
a JSON-LD offer availability value indicating stock

insufficient_evidence.form: "in stock" in prose
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Marketing copy is not the availability field a machine consumer reads, and it is frequently left behind when stock changes.

insufficient_evidence.form: a pre-order or back-order availability value
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The coffee is not immediately purchasable, which for a seasonal lot is a meaningful difference the buyer needs rather than a technicality.

insufficient_evidence.form: "restocked" or "new arrival" badges
insufficient_evidence.why_not: These are recency signals rather than availability, and inferring stock from them is how a stale page reads as current.

conflict_rules.when: structured data and the variant list disagree
conflict_rules.resolution: the engine reads structured data first and then the variant list, which is the precedence it already documents

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Sellers routinely hide or unpublish sold-out products, so a page a buyer can reach is usually purchasable. Seasonal micro-lots and pre-order harvest releases give this a real non-zero rate in coffee, but not enough to reach the fifteen per cent floor with confidence, so it is published rather than run. If a later measurement puts it inside the band it should be promoted, and that promotion would be a strengthening change needing no attestation.

entries.consumer_note: A coffee page you can reach is usually one you can buy from, so this rarely surprises anyone. The exception worth knowing is a pre-order for a new harvest, which is a real wait rather than a stock quirk.
entries.merchant_remediation: Expose availability in structured data with a purchasable offer, and mark harvest pre-orders as pre-order rather than as in stock so a machine consumer does not promise immediate dispatch.

citations.source: Google Merchant Center product data specification
citations.establishes: that availability is a required feed attribute with a defined enumeration including preorder and backorder, which is why the distinction between in stock and pre-order is treated as material by machine consumers

refutation.challenged: Whether this belongs in a standard at all given how rarely it fails.
refutation.resolution: It is published rather than run, in the same tier as price. The refuting pass did not identify availability as a shopper-driven coffee question, and the entry's demand basis is machine-consumer convention rather than buyer evidence, which is stated rather than dressed up.

entries.question: Can I buy a single bag without signing up for a recurring subscription?

applicability.applies_when: any purchasable coffee product

accepted_evidence.form: the absence of any statement that a subscription is required, which the engine reports as an inference rather than as proof

insufficient_evidence.form: "cancel anytime", "no commitment", "pause, skip or cancel"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Every one of these is a statement about exiting a subscription and is fully compatible with there being no one-time option at all, so treating them as reassurance inverts their meaning.

insufficient_evidence.form: a bare price with no billing period
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Subscription-only pages routinely display a price whose recurrence lives in a preselected radio label or a client-side widget, so a price is not evidence a one-time purchase exists.

insufficient_evidence.form: a "subscribe and save" badge
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It implies a comparison price without establishing that the comparison price is purchasable on its own.

insufficient_evidence.form: "add to cart" button text
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It is identical on subscription-only pages, so it carries no information about the purchase mode.

insufficient_evidence.form: the absence of the word subscription in the page source
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Subscription selectors are commonly injected client-side, so absence from server-rendered text is not evidence of absence from the page.

conflict_rules.when: a one-time option is present but disabled or out of stock
conflict_rules.resolution: the absence-based inference cannot see this at all, which is a limit of the assertion rather than a finding about the store

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: The engine searches only for explicit requirement phrasings such as "subscription required", which almost no page contains, and its own source records that this row therefore returns a passing state for very nearly everyone and would read as a guard that never fires. It is also the only requirement kind that can never produce evidenced proof, only an absence-based inference. Both facts point the same way and the row is published rather than run.

entries.consumer_note: Subscription-first selling is common in coffee and the phrase to distrust is "cancel anytime", which describes leaving a subscription rather than avoiding one. The check that works is whether a one-time option is selectable and priced before you enter payment details.
entries.merchant_remediation: State plainly that a one-time purchase is available and make it selectable without preselecting the recurring option, so a buyer does not have to infer the purchase mode from a radio button.

citations.source: US Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act, 15 USC 8403
citations.establishes: that a negative-option feature requires clear and conspicuous disclosure of all material terms before obtaining billing information, which makes default enrolment and undisclosed recurrence a regulated web-page failure rather than a design choice

citations.source: Internal measurement recorded in src/server/productTest.ts
citations.establishes: that the engine's own source records this row as returning a passing state unless a hard blocker is found, so its failure count is very nearly never non-zero and it would read as a guard that never fires

refutation.challenged: Whether the subscription class is well grounded at all, given that the research's only coffee-specific demand evidence was an uncited review.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass confirmed subscription mechanics as a verified shopper-driven core question on regulatory and search-intent grounds while finding that a complaint statistic the research leaned on could not be verified anywhere, and that the coffee-specific demand evidence was thin. The regulatory grounding is retained, the unverifiable statistic is not cited, and the row is published as not run because the engine's mechanism cannot detect the practice the law targets.

entries.question: Can I buy a decaf version of this same coffee?

applicability.applies_when: the seller offers caffeine choice as an option on this product

accepted_evidence.form: a purchasable option value naming the decaffeinated state

insufficient_evidence.form: a separate decaf product elsewhere in the catalogue
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A different product is not an option on this one, and this assertion can only see the offers attached to the page under test.

insufficient_evidence.form: "decaf available" in prose
insufficient_evidence.why_not: An availability statement is not a selectable option, and a buyer cannot complete the purchase from it.

insufficient_evidence.form: the word decaf in a collection handle or tag
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Merchant-controlled naming is assertion by labelling rather than evidence, and the engine deliberately never reads tags for category signals.

conflict_rules.when: decaf is sold as a separate product
conflict_rules.resolution: this entry fails and that failure is not a defect, which is precisely why the row is published rather than run
