predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Decaf is almost always a separate product rather than an option on a caffeinated one, because it is a different green lot processed at a different facility. A row failing for nearly everyone is the cruelty-free failure exactly: not false, but irrelevant, identical across unrelated merchants, and enough to make a specific diagnosis read like a template. Published so a reader can see it was considered and rejected on that ground.

entries.consumer_note: Decaf is normally a separate coffee rather than a switch on the one you are looking at, because the caffeine is removed from green beans at a specialist facility before roasting. If you want decaf, search for it as its own product.
entries.merchant_remediation: No remediation is implied. If you do offer the same lot in both states, exposing that as an option helps a buyer, but structuring decaf as a separate product is normal and correct.

citations.source: Coffee Intelligence, specialty coffee trade publication
citations.establishes: that decaffeination happens at a small number of specialist facilities on green coffee before roasting, and that US decaf consumption rose from nine to twelve per cent of the market in a year, so demand for decaf is real while it is structurally a separate product

refutation.challenged: Whether a near-certain failure should appear in a published standard at all.
refutation.resolution: It appears only in the not-run tier and only because the failure would be misread as a merchant defect. The substantive decaf questions a buyer does ask — which method, and whether a solvent was used — are published separately as blocked, because the engine has no mechanism for them.

entries.question: Is this coffee vegan and gluten-free?

applicability.applies_when: the product is unflavoured roasted coffee with no added ingredients
does_not_apply_when: flavoured coffee, coffee mixes and anything containing a creamer or a flavour system, where the question becomes real and the ingredient and allergen entries apply instead

accepted_evidence.form: an explicit dietary suitability statement in readable text

insufficient_evidence.form: the absence of an ingredients list
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Unflavoured coffee is a single-ingredient food, so nothing is expected there and absence is not evidence either way.

insufficient_evidence.form: "natural" or "clean" as a dietary signal
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Neither term has a dietary meaning, and neither excludes a flavour carrier that may contain a milk derivative.

insufficient_evidence.form: a facility statement such as "processed in a facility that also handles nuts"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A facility statement is voluntary precautionary wording rather than a declaration about this product.

conflict_rules.when: the product is flavoured and a dietary claim is made
conflict_rules.resolution: the ingredient and allergen entries govern; this entry does not apply and must not be read as covering it

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Plain roasted coffee is inherently both vegan and gluten-free, so almost no seller states it and the statement would carry no information if they did. This is the same vacuity an independent pass identified for kosher and non-GMO claims on unflavoured coffee, where a certifying body's own guidance says plain beans need no certification at all. Scoring a null as a trust signal is the failure this tier exists to prevent.

entries.consumer_note: Unflavoured roasted coffee contains only coffee, so it is vegan and gluten-free without anyone needing to say so. These questions become real for flavoured coffee, instant mixes and anything containing a creamer, where a flavour system can carry a milk derivative.
entries.merchant_remediation: No statement is needed for plain coffee. For flavoured coffee, publish the full ingredient declaration and emphasise any allergen, which is a legal requirement rather than a marketing choice.

citations.source: Star-K Kosher Certification, Knowing Your Beans: The Kashrus of Coffee
citations.establishes: that plain roasted coffee beans are inherently acceptable and need no certification because water is the only substance they contact, while all flavoured coffees do need it — a certifier stating that its own mark is uninformative on the plain product

citations.source: Non-GMO Project verification FAQ
citations.establishes: that verification targets ingredients derived from high-risk crops, with corn and soy as the named examples, and that coffee does not appear among them, so the mark is close to non-differentiating on single-ingredient coffee

refutation.challenged: Whether a question nobody asks about a property that is always true belongs in a published standard.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass independently reached the same conclusion for kosher and non-GMO claims on plain coffee, finding that coffee appears on neither the high-risk nor the monitored-risk crop list. Publishing the question with its reasoning is what stops a later author adding it as an executable trust signal, which is the specific mistake the tier prevents.

entries.question: How dark is this roast?

applicability.applies_when: the product is roasted coffee

accepted_evidence.form: a roast designation drawn from a stated scale, ideally with the scale named
a roast level exposed as a product option or specification row

insufficient_evidence.form: a roast level with no scale named
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Roast vocabulary is vendor-defined and the trade's own body concedes that City, Full City, French and Italian may be too arcane or flexible to be meaningful, so a bare word resolves against nothing.

insufficient_evidence.form: "Italian roast", "French roast", "Vienna roast"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: These are roast-degree style names that an origin extractor reads as geography, and Italian roast is the canonical false positive for a country-of-origin check.

insufficient_evidence.form: "bold", "strong", "full-bodied", "intensity 11"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Intensity scales grade roast and body rather than darkness or caffeine, and no scale behind them is published.

insufficient_evidence.form: a dark-roast description read as higher caffeine
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The inference runs opposite to how coffee is dosed by mass versus volume and is not a stated quantity in either direction.

insufficient_evidence.form: an instrumented colour number quoted for the roaster's equipment rather than this lot
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A capability figure for a machine is not a measurement of the coffee being sold.

conflict_rules.when: the option value and the description name different roast levels
conflict_rules.resolution: record both and report the contradiction; no external definition exists to arbitrate between them

registry.notes: An instrumented colour measure exists but is almost never published, and no register records a lot's roast level.

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Roast level is very commonly stated in some form, but stating it against a named scale is rare, so the band depends entirely on which of the two the assertion demands. A vocabulary matcher would sit at the low end and a scale requirement at the high end; that choice must be made when the mechanism is built.

entries.consumer_note: Of everything printed on a coffee label this is the detail specialty buyers say matters most, and it is also the one with no agreed scale: one roaster's medium is another's medium-dark. Reading the roaster's own scale, where they publish one, is the only way to compare across sellers.
entries.merchant_remediation: State the roast level and name the scale it is read against, and publish an instrumented colour value where you measure one, so the designation resolves against something other than house convention.

citations.source: Specialty Coffee Association
citations.establishes: that of all the information given on a coffee label, roast level is the most important to specialty coffee consumers — while the same body concedes that traditional roast names may be too arcane or flexible to be meaningful, which is exactly the tension this assertion has to encode

citations.source: Independent refuting pass, live search-intent retrieval
citations.establishes: that roast level ranks second of ten in the verified shopper-driven core, corroborated across the mainstream trade association and independent consumer studies rather than resting on specialty education material

refutation.challenged: Whether roast level is a shopper question or a roaster's descriptive habit.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass ranked it second of ten and verified the trade body's own statement that it is the most important label information to specialty consumers. It also verified the body conceding that the traditional names may be meaningless, which is why the assertion is specified as an enumerated value against a named scale rather than as keyword presence.

entries.question: How coarse is the grind, and what is that measured against?

applicability.applies_when: the product is sold ground or offers a grind choice
applicability.signal: a grind option or a grind designation in product text

accepted_evidence.form: a numeric particle-size range, or a named designation accompanied by the scale it is read against
a grind designation exposed as an option value

insufficient_evidence.form: a bare coarseness word such as medium or coarse
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It is a seller-relative label, two published scales disagree about it, and a consumer guide concedes on the record that fine, medium and coarse are neither universally acknowledged nor consistent.

insufficient_evidence.form: "standard grind", "regular grind", "universal grind", "all-purpose"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: This vocabulary names no point on any scale, and the immersion and espresso bands do not overlap, so no single grind can be universal.

insufficient_evidence.form: a grinder dial number or click count
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Grinder settings are proprietary and are not comparable across grinders or even across units of the same model.

insufficient_evidence.form: a brew-method name alone
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A method name does not pin a particle size, and the published espresso band alone spans roughly a factor of two.

insufficient_evidence.form: a micron figure quoted for the roaster's grinder or for a brewing guide elsewhere on the site
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A figure about equipment or a general guide is not a specification of what is in this bag.

conflict_rules.when: a numeric range and a brew-method recommendation disagree
conflict_rules.resolution: record the internal contradiction, which is the one thing a machine can check here without an external definition

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Almost no retail coffee page publishes a particle size or names the scale behind its grind word, so an assertion demanding either would fail for nearly everyone. That is a reason to specify it carefully rather than to run it as written: the useful executable form is the narrower question of whether a named grind option is purchasable, which is published separately, and this entry records the full question the buyer actually has.

entries.consumer_note: Grind size is the strongest single lever on how your coffee tastes and the words for it mean different things at different roasters. Until sellers publish a number or name their scale, matching a grind to your brewer from a page is guesswork.
entries.merchant_remediation: Publish a particle-size range or a sieve specification for each grind you sell, or at minimum name the scale your designations are read against, so a buyer can map your medium onto their brewer.

citations.source: Independent refuting pass, live search-intent retrieval
citations.establishes: that grind-to-brewer match is the strongest verified shopper signal in the corpus, with five of the top ten completions for coffee grind being brewer-specific and a grind size chart ranking first

citations.source: Specialty Coffee Association, coffee standards index
citations.establishes: that published trade standards cover grinders and brewers but define no retail grind designation vocabulary, so a grind word on a bag resolves against no external definition

refutation.challenged: Whether an assertion that would fail for nearly every seller is worth publishing.
refutation.resolution: It is published as blocked rather than run, and its own discrimination reasoning states the failure rate would be uninformative as written. The refuting pass ranked the underlying question first of ten, so omitting it would leave the strongest shopper signal in the corpus unrepresented in the document.

entries.question: How was the caffeine taken out of this coffee?

applicability.applies_when: the product is decaffeinated coffee
does_not_apply_when: caffeinated coffee, where the question does not arise
applicability.signal: undecidable_from_public_data — whether a product is decaf is itself one of the questions being asked, so this entry cannot be gated by the engine and must not fire on caffeinated coffee

accepted_evidence.form: an explicit named process attributed to this product, ideally in a labelled field such as a decaffeination row in a specification block
the same named process inside the JSON-LD product description

insufficient_evidence.form: a specification row labelled only "Process"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: On virtually every coffee page Process names the post-harvest treatment at the mill — washed, natural, honey — and says nothing about decaffeination, so a check keyed on that word reads a drying method as a solvent disclosure. This is the most dangerous near-miss in the entire standard.

insufficient_evidence.form: the word decaf or decaffeinated anywhere
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It establishes the product class and never the method, and it is the string a title, tag or collection handle is most likely to carry.

insufficient_evidence.form: "gently decaffeinated", "our proprietary decaf process", "premium decaf"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: These name no process and cannot be checked against anything.

insufficient_evidence.form: a method named on an About or FAQ page while this product is silent
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Roasters commonly stock more than one decaf origin processed at more than one facility, so a site-level statement does not establish a fact about this lot.

insufficient_evidence.form: "washed decaf"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: This means washed at origin AND decaffeinated by some means; it does not mean the caffeine was removed with water.

insufficient_evidence.form: the process named only in a customer review or question block
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A buyer's words are not the seller's statement, and the engine correctly refuses review context as evidence.

conflict_rules.when: a post-harvest process and a decaffeination method both appear
conflict_rules.resolution: the two are orthogonal and both may be stated; a checker must key on a decaf-scoped label rather than on the bare word process

conflict_rules.when: the page names a facility rather than a method
conflict_rules.resolution: a named processor is stronger evidence than a method word, because it makes the claim checkable by asking one company

registry.notes: No register records which method was used on a retail lot. A regulatory docket resolves whether a solvent remains authorised, which is a fact about the substance and not about any coffee.

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Specialty roasters increasingly name the method as a competitive signal while mainstream sellers almost never do, so the band spans two seller populations. Method disclosure is voluntary everywhere, which is the reason the question exists.

entries.consumer_note: There is no rule anywhere requiring a seller to say how the caffeine was removed, which is why a consumer-testing organisation tells readers to phone the supplier and ask. The methods differ materially — some use a chlorinated solvent, some an ester, some carbon dioxide, some only water and green coffee extract.
entries.merchant_remediation: Name the decaffeination process in a labelled field on the product page, distinct from the post-harvest process row, and name the facility where you know it, so a buyer can check by asking one company.

citations.source: Consumer Reports
citations.establishes: that there are no labelling rules requiring disclosure of how coffee was decaffeinated, and that consumers are advised to ask the supplier directly — advice written only because the demand exists and the label does not meet it

citations.source: National Geographic, reporting the Clean Label Project campaign
citations.establishes: that advocates are actively campaigning for coffee companies to list the decaffeination process on labels, which necessarily means it is not required today

citations.source: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Canadian Food Compositional Standards
citations.establishes: that a national compositional standard prescribes the common name for decaffeinated coffee and a caffeine ceiling while containing no requirement to declare the extraction solvent or process

refutation.challenged: Whether decaf method disclosure is a genuine shopper demand or a news-cycle artefact.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass ranked decaf third of ten in the verified shopper-driven core, citing verified consumer-organisation advice to phone the supplier, verified campaign coverage seeking on-label disclosure, and live autocomplete evidence for whether decaf is really decaf. The demand is current and independently corroborated.

entries.question: The page says chemical-free or naturally decaffeinated — what does that actually tell me?

applicability.applies_when: the page carries a chemical-free, solvent-free or naturally-decaffeinated claim on a decaffeinated product

accepted_evidence.form: a scoped, falsifiable negative tied to a named method, such as a statement that decaffeination used water and green coffee extract only with no chlorinated solvents and no esters

insufficient_evidence.form: "chemical-free" standing alone
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It is compatible with water, carbon dioxide and, on a self-serving reading, an ester process, and it is literally false of all of them, since water and carbon dioxide are chemicals. A regulator's guides treat a free-of claim as deceptive where the substance was never associated with the category.

insufficient_evidence.form: "naturally decaffeinated" or "natural decaf"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: This is the established trade euphemism for ethyl acetate, chosen because the compound occurs in fruit while the ester actually used is typically manufactured, so the phrase is compatible with the solvent process a buyer is trying to avoid.

insufficient_evidence.form: "solvent-free" applied to a water process
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Water is the solvent in a water process; the honest claim is that no chemical solvent was added, which is a different and narrower statement.

insufficient_evidence.form: "clean decaf", "pure decaf", "toxin-free", "no nasties"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: These are mood rather than method and name no process at all.

insufficient_evidence.form: a registered-trademark symbol beside a chemical-free phrase
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A trademark examination is not substantiation of a factual claim, yet the symbol reads to a shopper and to a naive check as validation.

insufficient_evidence.form: the absence of the phrase
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Silence is not evidence a solvent was used, so this assertion must never be inverted into an accusation.

conflict_rules.when: a chemical-free phrase appears with no named method anywhere on the page
conflict_rules.resolution: the claim fails rather than passes; a free-of claim with no method is the shape this entry exists to refuse

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Where the phrase appears at all it usually appears without a named method, so an assertion demanding substantiation would fail for most pages carrying the claim. The band is high because this entry is a refusal rule rather than a coverage rule, and its value is in denying a pass rather than in producing one.

entries.consumer_note: Chemical-free is not a category any regulator recognises, and naturally decaffeinated is the trade's usual wording for an ester solvent process. If you want assurance that no chemical solvent was added, look for a named water or carbon-dioxide process rather than for either phrase.
entries.merchant_remediation: Replace unscoped free-of wording with the named method and a scoped negative — for example that no chlorinated solvents and no esters were used — which is both checkable and defensible.

citations.source: US FTC Green Guides, 16 CFR 260.9
citations.establishes: that it is deceptive to misrepresent that a product is free of a substance, and that a literally true free-of claim can still deceive where the named substance was never associated with the product category — which is precisely the shape of a chemical-free food claim

citations.source: Consumer Reports
citations.establishes: that naturally decaffeinated does not assure the absence of a synthetic solvent, because producers use the term for ethyl acetate on the grounds that it occurs in fruit while the compound used is typically produced synthetically

refutation.challenged: Whether a standard should adjudicate a marketing phrase at all rather than simply ignoring it.
refutation.resolution: Ignoring it is what allows it to pass. Both the research and the refuting pass identified chemical-free as high-frequency, high-salience text that a keyword matcher will credit as a method assertion, so the standard's contribution here is an explicit refusal rule rather than a coverage rule.

entries.question: How much caffeine is actually left in this decaf?

assertion.subject: residual_caffeine
assertion.expected: a quantity with a stated basis

applicability.applies_when: the product is decaffeinated coffee

accepted_evidence.form: a residual-caffeine figure with its basis stated — a percentage of original caffeine, or a mass on a stated dry-weight or per-serving basis with the dose and volume named

insufficient_evidence.form: "caffeine free" or "naturally caffeine-free"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Decaffeinated coffee is never caffeine free under any construction, and a mainstream trade body puts the residue in the low milligrams per cup.

insufficient_evidence.form: "99.9% caffeine free" with no basis
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A percentage of what — the original caffeine, the bean mass, the brewed cup — changes the meaning by orders of magnitude, and the number looks well-formed either way.

insufficient_evidence.form: a milligram figure with no dose, water volume or brew method
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Without the inputs the number is not reproducible by the buyer and states nothing checkable.

insufficient_evidence.form: a percentage threshold quoted as a legal requirement
insufficient_evidence.why_not: There is no US standard of identity for decaffeinated roasted coffee and the commonly quoted removal figure originates with a trade association rather than a regulation, so citing it as law is wrong.

insufficient_evidence.form: "meets FDA standards"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The applicable federal provision caps a solvent residue rather than caffeine content, so the phrase reassures about a different question than the one asked.

insufficient_evidence.form: an EU threshold for coffee extract applied to whole beans
insufficient_evidence.why_not: That limit governs a different product, and applying it to roasted beans is a jurisdiction and product-scope error.

conflict_rules.when: a percentage and a milligram figure both appear
conflict_rules.resolution: record both with their bases; the standard reports the stated figures rather than converting between them

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Almost no retail decaf page publishes a residual figure with a basis, so this would fail for nearly everyone. It is published as blocked because the question is real and current, not because the assertion would be worth running as written.

entries.consumer_note: Decaf is not caffeine free, and how much remains varies. Any figure without its basis — per what dose, in what volume, measured how — cannot be reproduced or compared, which is why most stated numbers tell you nothing.
entries.merchant_remediation: If you have a laboratory result, publish the residual caffeine with its basis and the analysis date; otherwise state plainly that decaffeinated coffee retains a small amount rather than implying none.

citations.source: National Coffee Association
citations.establishes: that decaffeinated coffee retains a small measurable quantity of caffeine rather than none, which is the fact that makes caffeine-free wording on a decaf page false

citations.source: Independent refuting pass, live search-intent retrieval
citations.establishes: that whether decaf is really decaf, whether it is caffeine free, and whether it is safe in pregnancy are all live autocomplete completions, placing residual caffeine inside the verified shopper-driven decaf cluster

refutation.challenged: Whether the residual-caffeine question strays into health territory the standard has excluded.
refutation.resolution: It does adjoin it — the refuting pass found seven of ten decaf completions are health questions. The entry is therefore scoped strictly to whether a quantity with a basis is published, and it makes no assertion about physiological effect or suitability for anyone, which stays on the safe side of the exclusion recorded in out_of_scope.

entries.question: When was this roasted?

assertion.subject: roast_date
assertion.expected: an unambiguous calendar date bound to the act of roasting

applicability.applies_when: the product is roasted coffee sold by mass

accepted_evidence.form: an explicit calendar date bound on the page to roasting, in an unambiguous form
the same date inside the JSON-LD product description prose

insufficient_evidence.form: a roast LEVEL such as "Roast: Medium"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It contains the token roast next to a value and is the single most likely false positive for any automated check, because roast level is commonly exposed as an option or specification row while the date is not.

insufficient_evidence.form: "freshly roasted", "roasted weekly", "small-batch roasted"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Adjectives with no date, and unfalsifiable on the page.

insufficient_evidence.form: "roast date printed on every bag"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: This is an assertion about the bag rather than a date, and it is exactly the shape that defeats a check looking for the token roast date.

insufficient_evidence.form: a best-before, best-by or use-by date
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A durability estimate is not an age, and a long durability date coexisting with no roast date is the pattern buyers complain about.

insufficient_evidence.form: a packed-on or packaged-on date
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Packing lags roasting, and lags it by policy in rested-then-packed and gas-flushed operations.

insufficient_evidence.form: a harvest or crop year
insufficient_evidence.why_not: That is a green-coffee attribute unrelated to when the coffee was roasted.

insufficient_evidence.form: a structured production-date or feed expiration field
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The nearest structured-data property is vehicle-oriented and has no food semantics, and the dominant feed specification's expiration attribute controls when a listing stops showing and defaults to thirty days after the last refresh, so mapping either to freshness is categorically wrong and wrong in the flattering direction.

insufficient_evidence.form: a date visible only in a product photograph or a review image
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Image content is not page text, and product photography is frequently a stock image of a different size or an older bag.

conflict_rules.when: a roast date and a best-before date both appear
conflict_rules.resolution: treat them as answers to different questions and record both; a durability date can never be back-calculated to a roast day

conflict_rules.when: a static metafield holds a roast date
conflict_rules.resolution: treat it as low-trust: a field set once at product creation asserts something untrue about every subsequent lot, which is worse than no field

registry.notes: No register, no certificate holder, no auditor and no buyer-queryable lot traceability exists anywhere in the freshness class.

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: The roast date is a lot attribute stamped at pack time while a product page is a product-level document, so its absence is structural rather than negligent and should be near-universal. The band is above target and the entry is published as blocked partly for that reason: the honest contribution here is refusing the near-misses rather than certifying the claim.

entries.consumer_note: Specialty buyers look for a roast date because flavour changes over weeks, and consumer testing publications supply physical bag tests precisely because the date is so often absent. Note that the mainstream trade association points shoppers to the best-by date instead, so the trade does not agree with itself here.
entries.merchant_remediation: Publish the roast date for the lot currently shipping, in an unambiguous format, in a field you update as stock rotates — and keep it distinct from the roast level, which is a different fact that shares the word.

citations.source: America's Test Kitchen
citations.establishes: that mainstream consumer guidance tells readers roasters only sometimes print a roasted-on date and supplies a physical bag test to infer roast age, which is evidence the datum is frequently absent

citations.source: Perfect Daily Grind
citations.establishes: that roast date is a third-wave trade convention which the specialty trade press itself cautions against using as a sole quality signal — the source both grounds the demand and limits it

citations.source: Specialty Coffee Association, coffee standards index
citations.establishes: the decisive negative: no published trade standard covers roasted-coffee retail labelling, roast-date declaration, shelf life or freshness, so citing the trade body for roast date is unsupported

refutation.challenged: Whether roast-date demand is real shopper behaviour or a preference the trade taught its own customers, and whether any trade organisation's published standards back it.
refutation.resolution: No body backs it — the trade body publishes nothing on retail labelling or freshness, and the trade press itself records that third-wave roasters taught consumers to buy on roast date. Demand is well evidenced among enthusiasts and not established for mainstream buyers, whose own trade association points them at the best-by date instead. The entry therefore carries a trade-convention warning label in its demand basis alongside the community and consumer-guide evidence.

entries.question: If there is a date on this, is it worded the way the law where I live requires?

applicability.applies_when: the page displays a quality or safety date phrase for the product
applicability.signal: presence of a date phrase in product text

accepted_evidence.form: a date phrase matching a jurisdiction's enumerated literal, captured verbatim with the matched jurisdiction named

insufficient_evidence.form: informal variants such as "Best by", "Expires", "Enjoy by", "Freshest by"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: None matches the enumerated forms either regime requires, and their familiarity is what makes them look compliant.

insufficient_evidence.form: "Best before" treated as globally acceptable
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It is the EU-required form and is not among the phrases the Californian regime enumerates, so the two regimes demand different literals and a single phrase cannot satisfy both — a check that treats it as universally compliant will pass a violation.

insufficient_evidence.form: "Sell by" on a consumer-facing page
insufficient_evidence.why_not: That phrase is prohibited outright in the Californian regime for consumer-facing use, with a narrow exception for coded inventory dates not readily readable by consumers.

insufficient_evidence.form: the absence of any date read as non-compliance
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Adding a date is not mandated by either regime for this product, and the Californian statute expressly disclaims that construction — so reporting absence as a defect would be a false positive with a legal citation attached, which is the worst kind.

insufficient_evidence.form: a conformance verdict presented as a legal finding about the physical label
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The regime governs the labelling of a food item offered for sale; whether a page reproducing a non-conforming phrase is itself a violation could not be established, so the verdict is about the page string only.

conflict_rules.when: a page serves both markets with one date phrase
conflict_rules.resolution: record that the phrase cannot satisfy both enumerated sets, which is a factual observation rather than a legal conclusion

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Applies only to pages that display a date phrase at all, and within that population informal wording is common, so a genuine split is plausible. This is the most crisply machine-checkable assertion in the whole freshness class, because both regimes specify closed sets of literal phrases rather than concepts.

entries.consumer_note: Date wording is regulated because shoppers cannot reliably tell a quality date from a safety date, and the required phrasing differs between regions. A page that says nothing about dates is not breaking any rule; a page that says "sell by" to a consumer may be.
entries.merchant_remediation: Where you display a quality or safety date, use the exact phrase your market's rules enumerate, and avoid consumer-facing sell-by wording; if you serve two markets with different required literals, the page needs market-specific wording.

citations.source: California Assembly Bill 660, statutory text
citations.establishes: an enumerated set of permitted quality and safety date phrases for food items manufactured on or after 1 July 2026, a blanket prohibition on consumer-facing sell-by wording, and an express disclaimer that the section does not require a date label — coffee is in scope

citations.source: EU Regulation 1169/2011, Annex X point 1(a)
citations.establishes: the conflicting EU wording requirement of Best before with a day, or Best before end otherwise, which is not among the Californian permitted phrases

citations.source: National Agricultural Law Center, University of Arkansas
citations.establishes: independent confirmation that no federal requirement mandates date labels on most foods and that including a date remains voluntary unless another law requires it

refutation.challenged: Whether a law-firm summary asserting the Californian regime mandates a date label should be preferred to the statutory text, and whether the regime reaches a web page at all.
refutation.resolution: The statute governs and expressly disclaims a mandate, so the summary was not followed. Whether a page reproducing a phrase is itself a violation could not be established from cited authority, so the entry's verdict is explicitly scoped to the page string and is not presented as a legal finding — and the refuting pass separately confirmed that both underlying legal readings in the freshness class hold up.

entries.question: How should I store this once it arrives, and should I keep it in the fridge or freezer?

applicability.applies_when: the product is roasted coffee sold to a consumer

accepted_evidence.form: storage conditions with the parameters that matter — container type, a temperature or range, and explicit direction on refrigeration and freezing
the same guidance in FAQ structured data attached to this product

insufficient_evidence.form: "store in a cool, dry place"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Generic boilerplate with no temperature that is silent on the refrigeration question buyers actually have, and arguably not a special condition at all.

insufficient_evidence.form: "keep sealed" or "reseal after opening"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Closure handling is not a storage condition, and the two are routinely conflated in copy.

insufficient_evidence.form: advice to refrigerate for longer life
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It runs directly contrary to mainstream trade-association guidance, so presence of storage advice must not be scored as soundness of storage advice; presence and correctness are different tests.

insufficient_evidence.form: a freezing recommendation with no airtight-container and small-portion caveats
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Those caveats are what make freezing survivable rather than harmful, so the recommendation without them is incomplete.

insufficient_evidence.form: guidance living only in a blog post or brewing guide
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Where the pre-purchase distance-selling requirement applies the information must be available in connection with the offer, so location matters and a blog is not the offer.

conflict_rules.when: the page recommends refrigeration and the trade body advises against it
conflict_rules.resolution: record that guidance is present and do not adjudicate whether it is sound; the standard reports evidence availability, not correctness

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Storage guidance is common in some form but rarely carries a temperature or addresses refrigeration explicitly, so the band depends on how strictly the parameters are required. The vocabulary is small and stable, which makes this unusually tractable to match once a mechanism exists.

entries.consumer_note: This is the freshness question with a real legal hook behind it in the EU, and the one where popular advice is most often wrong: the mainstream trade association strongly advises against refrigerating coffee, and the trade's own assessment protocol says to store it cool and dark but not refrigerated or frozen.
entries.merchant_remediation: State storage conditions on the product page rather than in a blog — container type, a temperature range, and explicit direction on refrigeration and freezing with the caveats that make freezing safe.

citations.source: EU Regulation 1169/2011, Article 9(1)(g) and Article 14(1)(a)
citations.establishes: that special storage conditions are a mandatory particular and, unlike the durability date, are NOT carved out of the pre-purchase distance-selling requirement — making storage the strongest legally-grounded hook for a coffee product page in the whole freshness class

citations.source: National Coffee Association, storage and shelf life guidance
citations.establishes: substantive guidance to keep coffee away from air, moisture, heat and light in an opaque airtight container at room temperature, with refrigeration strongly advised against, which is what makes the refrigeration direction the decisive parameter

citations.source: Independent refuting pass, live search-intent retrieval
citations.establishes: that how to store coffee beans after opening, to keep them fresh, and whether to use the fridge are all live autocomplete completions, placing storage inside the verified shopper-driven core

refutation.challenged: Whether the pre-purchase storage duty is a real reading of the distance-selling provision or an over-reach borrowed from package labelling.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass set out to break this reading and could not: the pre-purchase carve-out names only the durability date, so storage conditions do fall within the pre-purchase requirement. It called the corollary a correct and non-obvious reading and the best analytical work in the research corpus. Whether roasted coffee's storage needs qualify as special remains a judgement no source addressed, and this entry does not assert that they do.

entries.question: Which country was this coffee grown in?

applicability.applies_when: the product is roasted coffee

accepted_evidence.form: a named growing country attributed to this coffee, distinct from where it was roasted
the same statement inside the JSON-LD product description

insufficient_evidence.form: "Product of USA", "Made in USA", "Roasted in USA"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Under customs substantial-transformation practice these describe ROASTING, so a check that maps them to growing origin will systematically record Ethiopian coffee as American. The legally correct origin marking is the one that hides the answer buyers want, and this is the highest-value trap in the whole standard.

insufficient_evidence.form: "Italian roast", "French roast", "Vienna roast"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: These are roast-degree style names, and Italian roast is the canonical false positive for any origin extractor.

insufficient_evidence.form: "Imported"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It satisfies a marking requirement while naming no country at all.

insufficient_evidence.form: a region, farm, washing station or varietal name with no country
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Evocative and unresolvable; several region names exist in more than one country and some varietal names are also place names.

insufficient_evidence.form: "Latin American blend" or "African blend"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A region is not a country, and blend composition legitimately varies batch to batch.

insufficient_evidence.form: a flag emoji or graphic
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Not page text, not read by the engine, and frequently decorative rather than a claim.

conflict_rules.when: a roasting location and a growing country both appear
conflict_rules.resolution: attribute each to its own act; a roasting statement must never satisfy a growing-origin assertion

conflict_rules.when: the product is a blend naming several countries
conflict_rules.resolution: record all named origins; "a place is stated" and "the origin of this coffee is stated" are different questions and the second is the one asked

registry.notes: Regulatory traceability that would come closest — plot-level geolocation filed as a due-diligence statement — is not a public lookup.

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Specialty coffee names origins constantly while supermarket-style listings often do not, so a real split exists. The band is a hypothesis about two seller populations and the engine has no mechanism to measure it, which is why the entry is blocked rather than predicted with confidence.

entries.consumer_note: Where coffee is roasted and where it is grown are different facts, and the phrase you are most likely to see on a US bag describes roasting. If the page names no growing country, no amount of made-in wording fills that gap.
entries.merchant_remediation: Name the growing country in product text, keeping it clearly distinct from any statement about where the coffee was roasted, and add the region where you know it.

citations.source: US Customs and Border Protection, country-of-origin marking practice on roasting as substantial transformation
citations.establishes: that roasting imported green coffee is treated as substantially transforming it, which is why product-of-USA wording on a coffee bag describes roasting and not growing — the mechanism behind the standard's most consequential false-positive risk

citations.source: Independent refuting pass, live search-intent retrieval
citations.establishes: that grown-versus-roasted origin sits in the verified shopper-driven core, grounded in documented deception rather than in query volume

refutation.challenged: Whether the origin question can be built at all, given that the engine removed its origin matcher for being wrong in both directions.
refutation.resolution: The question survives and the mechanism does not. The engine's removed matcher failed on real copy in both directions and its own record forbids a third head-noun rule, so this entry is published as blocked with the measured path back recorded in ENGINE_GAPS G-01 rather than specified as though it worked.

entries.question: How was this coffee processed after picking — washed, natural, or honey?

applicability.applies_when: the product is roasted coffee whose page discusses origin processing

accepted_evidence.form: a named process class drawn from the international coffee vocabulary and attributed to this lot, ideally with the defining step described

insufficient_evidence.form: the bare word "processed" or "artisan processed"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: All coffee is processed, so the word is content-free.

insufficient_evidence.form: "sun-dried" or "patio dried" read as natural
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Washed coffee is also sun-dried on beds or patios, so the drying medium does not identify the process class.

insufficient_evidence.form: "semi-washed" treated as a synonym for honey
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Semi-washed is mechanical demucilage while honey retains the mucilage; they are near-opposites on the one variable that matters.

insufficient_evidence.form: yellow, red or black honey treated as a graded scale
insufficient_evidence.why_not: No body defines the mucilage proportion or the colour boundaries, so the words encode nothing standardised.

insufficient_evidence.form: a process word inside a tasting-note sentence
insufficient_evidence.why_not: "Notes of honey" states a flavour and "washed with bright acidity" describes mouthfeel; these are the commonest sentences on a specialty page and a bare vocabulary match reads every one as a process statement.

insufficient_evidence.form: the process named for the roaster's buying programme rather than this lot
insufficient_evidence.why_not: "We buy washed coffees" is a sourcing statement and does not establish what this bag is.

conflict_rules.when: a post-harvest process and a decaffeination method both appear
conflict_rules.resolution: they are orthogonal; a process row must never be read as a decaffeination disclosure

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Specialty pages name the process routinely and mainstream pages almost never do, so the split is real but entirely population-dependent. The tasting-note collision means a naive matcher would report a much lower failure rate than the truth.

entries.consumer_note: Processing is the step that most changes how a coffee tastes for a given origin, and the words for it are defined in an international vocabulary for the two main classes. Honey and its colour variants are not defined anywhere, so those describe intent rather than a specification.
entries.merchant_remediation: Name the process class in a labelled field and describe the defining step for anything outside the two standard classes, because honey and fermentation variants have no external definition to appeal to.

citations.source: ISO 3509 coffee and coffee products vocabulary
citations.establishes: that an international vocabulary defines the washed and natural process classes, which is what makes those two checkable against an external definition while honey and wet-hulled are not defined in it at all

refutation.challenged: Whether shoppers ask about processing method or whether this is producer and student intent.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass found that processing-method autocomplete returns plant, equipment and flow-chart results, indicating producer and student intent rather than shopper intent, and placed the whole specialty-provenance tier as largely trade-invented on the grounds that its sources define terms rather than evidence demand. The entry is retained as blocked because a definition genuinely exists for the two main classes, but its demand basis claims no buyer-community evidence and the finer provenance questions were dropped — recorded in GROUNDING.md.

entries.question: Does the weight shown apply to the exact size I am buying?

applicability.applies_when: the product page sells more than one purchasable size
applicability.signal: more than one variant with distinct option values

accepted_evidence.form: a net quantity resolved per purchasable offer, either in the option value itself or in per-offer structured data

insufficient_evidence.form: a weight in the page title on a multi-size page
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The classic false pass: the title says twelve ounces while the selected variant is five pounds, and the title is a quotable evidence surface so a check credits it.

insufficient_evidence.form: the first or the largest weight on the page
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Option order is arbitrary and the most prominent size is often the best-value one the seller wants to feature, so neither is the buyer's offer.

insufficient_evidence.form: a subscription or bundle offer's values applied to the single-bag offer
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Those are different offers at different quantities, and conflating them misstates what the buyer receives.

insufficient_evidence.form: group-level structured data inherited from one representative variant
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A product-group node describes the group, and its values were taken from whichever variant happened to populate them.

insufficient_evidence.form: a sold-out variant included in the resolution
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A size offered but unbuyable is not what the buyer receives.

conflict_rules.when: no default selection is determinable
conflict_rules.resolution: report the claim as ambiguous across offers rather than resolving it to any one size; there is currently no result state for that, which is part of what blocks this entry

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Multi-size coffee pages are common and per-offer quantity resolution is rare, so a real split is likely among the pages this applies to. The band excludes single-offer pages, where the question does not arise.

entries.consumer_note: On a page selling several bag sizes, the weight in the title belongs to one of them and not necessarily the one you selected. This is how a price comparison silently goes wrong by a factor of several.
entries.merchant_remediation: Carry the net quantity in each purchasable option value or in per-offer structured data, so the weight travels with the offer rather than sitting once at page level.

citations.source: EU Regulation 1169/2011, Article 14(1)(a)
citations.establishes: that mandatory particulars other than the durability date must be available before the purchase is concluded, which for a multi-offer page means available for the offer actually being purchased rather than for the page in general

citations.source: Independent refuting pass, live search-intent retrieval
citations.establishes: that cost transparency including net weight sits in the verified shopper-driven core, which is what makes per-offer resolution a buyer concern rather than a data-modelling nicety

entries.question: What does this cost per kilogram, so I can compare it with another bag?

expected.rule: price divided by net mass for the same offer

applicability.applies_when: the product is coffee sold by mass with a readable price
applicability.signal: a readable price and a readable net quantity for the same offer

accepted_evidence.form: a price for the offer, in the same currency and tax treatment as the selling price
a net quantity for the same offer, from which the unit price is computable

insufficient_evidence.form: value language such as "great value" or "cheaper than your coffee shop"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: No arithmetic is available, so nothing can be compared.

insufficient_evidence.form: a price per pod or per serving
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Dose per capsule varies by roughly a factor of two across systems, so a per-item rate is not a rate per unit mass.

insufficient_evidence.form: a rate computed on gross or shipping weight
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Those include packaging and are systematically high, so the derived figure is wrong in a direction that flatters the seller.

insufficient_evidence.form: a rate computed on the wrong variant
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The classic case is the large size's better rate displayed against a small-size selection, which is exactly the comparison the buyer is trying to make.

insufficient_evidence.form: a rate derived from a strikethrough or reference price
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A price the seller never charged cannot be the basis of a cost comparison.

conflict_rules.when: the net quantity cannot be attributed to the priced offer
conflict_rules.resolution: refuse to derive a figure rather than computing one from mismatched inputs; a derived number reads as more authoritative than the sentence it came from

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Both inputs are individually common and their attribution to the same offer is not, so the derived assertion should fail materially more often than either input alone. Any derived value inherits every weakness of its inputs, and the net-quantity input has pinned defects, so this is the entry most likely to produce a confidently wrong number.

entries.consumer_note: Price per kilogram is the only way to compare two bags of different sizes, and it is the figure most often missing. If the page shows a price and a weight you can divide them yourself, provided both belong to the size you selected.
entries.merchant_remediation: Display the unit price alongside the selling price for each purchasable size, computed on net mass in the same currency and tax treatment as the price shown.

citations.source: EU Directive 98/6/EC on the indication of prices of products offered to consumers
citations.establishes: that both the selling price and the unit price must be indicated for products sold by mass, making unit price a regulated consumer-facing disclosure rather than a convenience

refutation.challenged: Whether shoppers actually use unit prices, as opposed to regulators requiring them.
refutation.resolution: The research volunteered against its own interest here, recording that the requirement is strongly mandated and weakly demonstrated as behaviour, and the refuting pass credited that honesty. The entry's demand basis therefore claims regulatory and comparison-convention grounding and no buyer-community evidence, and it is blocked rather than run in any case.

entries.question: Is there anything in this besides coffee?

applicability.applies_when: the product contains anything beyond roasted coffee — flavourings, sugar, chicory, other grains, or a creamer
does_not_apply_when: unflavoured single-ingredient roasted coffee, where no declaration is expected
applicability.signal: undecidable_from_public_data — whether anything was added is itself the question being asked

accepted_evidence.form: a complete ingredient declaration in descending order of weight, in a labelled field rather than in marketing prose
the same declaration inside the JSON-LD product description

insufficient_evidence.form: "100% Arabica"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: That is a botanical species claim rather than an ingredient declaration, and a hundred-per-cent-arabica coffee can still be flavoured.

insufficient_evidence.form: "100% coffee" in marketing prose
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The same words in prose and in an ingredients field have different legal functions, and a text match cannot tell them apart.

insufficient_evidence.form: "no additives", "no fillers", "nothing but beans"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Negative marketing claims are not the positive declaration the rule requires, and they are unverifiable as stated.

insufficient_evidence.form: "natural flavour" listed without the base ingredient
insufficient_evidence.why_not: An incomplete list reads as a complete one, which is worse than no list for a reader trying to check.

insufficient_evidence.form: an ingredient list scraped from a different variant on a multi-variant page
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The flavoured variant's list shown against the unflavoured one asserts something false about the offer being bought.

insufficient_evidence.form: a photograph of the back panel
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Image content is not machine-readable, so a text-only check would score a compliant page as non-compliant — a false positive rather than a finding.

insufficient_evidence.form: "unflavoured" where flavour was introduced before roasting
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Flavour added at green stage sits outside the reasoning a flavour-labelling check would apply, so the word can be true in the seller's mind and misleading to the buyer.

conflict_rules.when: the page is silent and the product may or may not be flavoured
conflict_rules.resolution: the entry does not apply; silence on a single-ingredient food is expected and must never be reported as a missing declaration

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Among flavoured coffee pages a full declaration in a labelled field is far from universal, so a real split is plausible. The band applies only to the products this entry covers, and the applicability signal being undecidable from public data is itself part of what blocks it.

entries.consumer_note: Plain coffee is a single-ingredient food and needs no list, so an absent list is normal. For a flavoured coffee it is the only way to know what you are drinking, and a flavour system can carry things a shopper would want to know about.
entries.merchant_remediation: For anything beyond plain roasted coffee, publish the complete ingredient declaration in a labelled field on the product page, and keep each variant's declaration attached to that variant.

citations.source: EU Regulation 1169/2011, Article 9(1)(b) and Article 14(1)(a)
citations.establishes: that the list of ingredients is a mandatory particular and must be available before the purchase is concluded in distance selling, since only the durability date is carved out — which makes this a genuine pre-purchase page duty rather than a package-only rule

refutation.challenged: Whether the ingredient duty reaches a web page or only the physical pack, given that the same research mislabelled US net-quantity law as a page duty.
refutation.resolution: It reaches the page in the EU by the same Article 14(1)(a) route that the refuting pass verified for storage conditions, and the entry cites that route rather than US package-labelling law. The refuting pass independently listed flavourings and allergens as mandated pre-purchase and as the one thing a certifier's own consumer coffee article says actually matters.

entries.question: Does this contain anything I am allergic to?

applicability.applies_when: the product is flavoured coffee or contains any added ingredient

accepted_evidence.form: the regulated allergen named within the ingredient declaration and emphasised, rather than mentioned separately

insufficient_evidence.form: "may contain traces of"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Precautionary wording is voluntary and is not the declaration the rule requires, so a check that accepts it treats a hedge as a disclosure.

insufficient_evidence.form: "dairy-free", "gluten-free", "vegan"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: These are free-from and lifestyle claims governed by different rules; none is an allergen declaration and vegan says nothing about cross-contact.

insufficient_evidence.form: "naturally flavoured" with no carrier named
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Flavour systems commonly carry milk derivatives, and the word natural excludes nothing.

insufficient_evidence.form: "processed in a facility that also handles nuts"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A facility statement describes the plant rather than this product.

insufficient_evidence.form: "allergens: none" on a flavoured product with no readable ingredient list
insufficient_evidence.why_not: An unverifiable negative, and the shape most likely to be scored as a complete disclosure.

insufficient_evidence.form: the absence of emphasis in scraped text
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Emphasis is legally required inside an EU ingredient list, and stripped markup loses it — so a page can be compliant while the extracted text is not evidently so, which a check must not report as a defect.

conflict_rules.when: emphasis cannot be recovered from the extracted text
conflict_rules.resolution: report that the emphasis could not be inspected rather than that it is absent; this is the not-inspectable versus not-present distinction the engine already enforces elsewhere

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Among flavoured coffee pages, a properly emphasised allergen inside a full declaration is uncommon in web copy even where the physical pack is compliant. The band applies only to products with added ingredients.

entries.consumer_note: For plain coffee this does not arise. For a flavoured coffee it matters, and the reassurance you should not rely on is a may-contain line, which is voluntary wording rather than a declaration.
entries.merchant_remediation: Name the regulated allergen inside the ingredient declaration with the emphasis the rule requires, on the product page and per variant, rather than in a separate reassurance sentence.

citations.source: EU Regulation 1169/2011, Article 9(1)(c), Article 21 and Article 14(1)(a)
citations.establishes: that substances causing allergies must be indicated in the ingredient list with emphasis distinguishing them from the other ingredients, and that this particular is available pre-purchase in distance selling because only the durability date is excluded

refutation.challenged: Whether allergens are a coffee question at all.
refutation.resolution: Not for plain coffee, and the entry's applicability now excludes it explicitly. For flavoured coffee the refuting pass ranked flavourings and allergens tenth of ten in the verified shopper core and noted it is mandated pre-purchase, so the entry is retained with a narrowed envelope.

entries.question: Does the organic claim on this page resolve against the certifier's own public register?

applicability.applies_when: the page states an organic claim and names a certifying agent
applicability.signal: an organic claim plus a named agent in product text

accepted_evidence.form: a record for the seller's legal operation with status Certified as of the sale date, whose certified-product scope covers handled or processed coffee
the certifying agent's name and the certified legal operation name published on the page, which are the two keys a lookup needs

insufficient_evidence.form: a certificate PDF hosted on the seller's own domain
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Self-published is not the register, and the register exists precisely because a document can outlive the certification it describes.

insufficient_evidence.form: a genuine, well-formatted certificate whose validity period has ended
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The most convincing-looking near-miss there is, and the exact case the register's surrendered, suspended and revoked statuses exist to catch.

insufficient_evidence.form: a register hit on a similarly-named entity
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A brand or trading name matched against a different legal operation is fuzzy entity resolution rather than a lookup, and it invents its own evidence.

insufficient_evidence.form: a hit whose certified-product scope excludes handling
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A crops-only record does not authorise a roaster's organic label, so scope match matters as much as status.

insufficient_evidence.form: a farm's or exporter's certificate offered for the roaster
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Only a certified handler may use the seal, so the register must resolve to the entity on the label.

insufficient_evidence.form: "not found in the register" rendered as a false claim
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A roaster can legitimately sell certified coffee without holding a certificate itself, and rendering absence as falsity would be the worst false statement this product could make about a store.

conflict_rules.when: the register is unreachable
conflict_rules.resolution: produce an honest unreachable state rather than degrading to a failure; an unreachable register must never look like a failed lookup

conflict_rules.when: the page publishes no certificate number
conflict_rules.resolution: treat the absence as a page finding rather than as a failed lookup, because no number is required on the label and fuzzy-matching a brand to a holder is not verification

registry.register_name: USDA National Organic Program — Organic INTEGRITY Database
registry.lookup_key: the certified operation's legal name, client ID or certificate number
registry.lookup_method: Search by operation name, certifying agent, certified product, client ID or certificate number; read the status enum, the effective dates and the certified-products list. Bulk spreadsheet exports and monthly full-dataset snapshots were confirmed live by an independent verification pass; the documented REST API was not, because its developer help page returns an application error.
registry.notes: This is the strongest register in coffee and the only one that is simultaneously mandated on-label, resolvable to the seller, status-typed, certificate-downloadable and available in bulk. If the engine ever supports exactly one registry assertion, it should be this one.

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Most pages that claim organic publish neither the certifying agent's name nor the certified legal entity, so the lookup would have no key and the assertion would fail for most of the population it applies to. The failure would usually be a page-disclosure finding rather than a certification finding, which is a distinction the assertion must preserve.

entries.consumer_note: You can do this check yourself today, free, in the public register: search the roaster's legal name and read the status and the certified-product scope. What stops it being automatic is that pages publish brand names while the register holds legal operation names.
entries.merchant_remediation: Publish the certifying agent's name and your certified legal operation name — and the certificate number if you have one — so that a reader can resolve the claim deterministically rather than by guesswork.

citations.source: CCOF, guidance on using the Organic INTEGRITY Database
citations.establishes: that a certifying agent authorised under the national organic programme describes the register as the official place to check whether an operation is certified, and positions checking it as ongoing supplier management and fraud prevention rather than as a shopper task

citations.source: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service, organic enforcement settlements index
citations.establishes: that the regulator maintains an ongoing published record of settlements for organic misrepresentation, which is the regulator's own evidence that absent or lapsed certification coexists with live organic labelling

refutation.challenged: Whether shoppers verify certificates, or whether the entire verification tier is importer and retail-buyer behaviour dressed as consumer demand.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass established the latter: every look-it-up question traces to a certifier's own business-to-business material, one of them titled for checking a supplier's status. This entry therefore carries a trade-convention warning label in its demand basis and is blocked rather than executable, so the grammar's rule against executable entries resting on trade convention alone is respected rather than circumvented. The register itself was independently confirmed live, including a real bulk export.

entries.question: If this says Kona or Hawaiian, how much of it actually is?

applicability.applies_when: the page uses a Hawaii geographic coffee name in the product name, brand or description
applicability.signal: a Hawaii geographic coffee name in merchant-controlled text

accepted_evidence.form: the percentage of the named Hawaii origin, stated as a front-of-pack-equivalent disclosure rather than buried in body copy
the percentage adjacent to the geographic name in the product name

insufficient_evidence.form: "Kona Blend" with no percentage
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Historically the exact practice the legislation targets, and the shape a buyer is least equipped to read.

insufficient_evidence.form: "Kona-style", "Kona roast", "in the Kona tradition", "Hawaiian roast"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Geographic-name evocation without an origin claim, which is the concern behind the more recent amendment.

insufficient_evidence.form: a percentage stated deep in body copy rather than as a prominent disclosure
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The number is present and the disclosure test still fails, because the requirement is about prominence as well as presence.

insufficient_evidence.form: the roaster's Hawaii address inferred as Hawaii-grown coffee
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A business location says nothing about where the green coffee was grown, and this is the same roasting-versus-growing conflation as the general origin trap.

insufficient_evidence.form: "100% Kona" with nothing behind it
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The strongest-sounding string is also the least verifiable, since no public register resolves a bag's Hawaii content.

conflict_rules.when: the geographic name appears in the brand name rather than the description
conflict_rules.resolution: read merchant-controlled naming as within scope for the disclosure question, because a check confined to the description misses it entirely

conflict_rules.when: the applicable threshold changes on a date
conflict_rules.resolution: version the assertion; a disclosure that satisfied an earlier threshold does not satisfy a later one and the standard must state which it applied

registry.notes: Despite substantial litigation over Kona mislabelling, no public register resolves a given product's Hawaii content; the origin certificate is a document held by the trade rather than a searchable record.

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Applies only to pages using a Hawaii coffee name, and within that population percentage disclosure is inconsistent. The band is wide because the population is small and self-selecting, and because litigation pressure may have moved practice in ways this document cannot measure.

entries.consumer_note: A blend using a Hawaii coffee name may contain only a small fraction of it, and the required percentage is the only thing that tells you which. There is no public register you can check, so the page's own disclosure is all a buyer has.
entries.merchant_remediation: State the percentage of the named Hawaii origin prominently next to the geographic name wherever it appears, including in the product or brand name, and keep it current against the applicable threshold.

citations.source: Hawaii Revised Statutes chapter 486, coffee labelling provisions
citations.establishes: that Hawaii regulates the use of a Hawaii geographic origin name on coffee with a minimum content threshold and a disclosure requirement, which is what makes the percentage the checkable element rather than the name

refutation.challenged: Whether the protected-origin class is registry-resolvable as the research claimed, and whether the specific threshold and its effective date could be verified.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass called this the worst bundling in the research corpus: four structurally different things shared one registry-resolvable verdict, and the one they led with has no register at all — the research's own text conceded the origin certificate is a trade document rather than a public searchable register. The refuter was also bot-blocked from the legislature and could not confirm the amended threshold, so this entry states the mechanism and deliberately names no numeric threshold.

entries.question: How long should I let these beans rest before brewing them?

applicability.applies_when: the product is whole-bean roasted coffee
applicability.signal: product text discusses degassing or resting

accepted_evidence.form: a rest or peak window with explicit units and an explicit anchor to the roast date, attributed as this roaster's own recommendation

insufficient_evidence.form: a rest figure attributed to a trade organisation's published standards
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The only trade-anchored rest figure that exists is a cupping sample-preparation requirement for assessment within a day of roasting, and transplanting it to a shopper's brewing advice inverts its meaning. This is the near-miss most likely to be dressed in authority.

insufficient_evidence.form: a rest window with no roast date to anchor it
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A window measured from an unstated roast day is unactionable, and it is the commonest shape.

insufficient_evidence.form: "let rest a few days" or "allow to degas"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: No units, so nothing can be acted on or checked.

insufficient_evidence.form: any single number presented as the industry standard
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Published sources span three to thirty days and disagree openly, and the best-designed study located contradicts the professional norm it tested.

insufficient_evidence.form: a rest claim inferred from the presence of a valve
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A valve manages gas escape and bounds nothing about the coffee's age or readiness.

conflict_rules.when: a rest window and a peak window are both stated
conflict_rules.resolution: record both with their units; the standard reports the seller's stated guidance and declines to adjudicate the number

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Few pages state a window with units and an anchor, and no external definition exists to check the number against, so this is published as advisory rather than as something to run. Degassing is a real measurable physical process; the consumer window is not a settled quantity.

entries.consumer_note: Freshly roasted beans release gas for days and can taste better after a rest, but the trade genuinely disagrees about how long, with published advice spanning three to thirty days. Any single number offered as the industry standard is overstating a real disagreement.
entries.merchant_remediation: State your own recommended window with units, anchored to the roast date, and present it as your recommendation rather than as a settled figure.

citations.source: Smrke and others, Time-Resolved Gravimetric Method To Assess Degassing of Roasted Coffee, Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry
citations.establishes: that degassing is a real measurable physical process with mechanistic modelling behind it, tied to freshness, packaging and extraction — while the published abstract supplies no consumer-facing day counts

citations.source: Perfect Daily Grind
citations.establishes: that the trade documents its own disagreement rather than resolving it, with prime windows quoted variously as eight to twenty-one days and up to thirty, and some claiming a peak at three

refutation.challenged: Whether a rest window is a shopper concern or a barista one, and whether any authority backs a number.
refutation.resolution: No authority backs a number, and the entry is advisory as a result. Buyer-community threads do show shoppers timing their brewing against a roast date, so the question is retained, but its value depends entirely on the roast date being published — which is itself blocked.

entries.question: How long will this stay good, and does that change once I open the bag?

applicability.applies_when: the product is roasted coffee sold by mass

accepted_evidence.form: separate windows for unopened and after-opening, each with units, each stated for the grind state being sold

insufficient_evidence.form: an unopened-pack shelf life quoted as if it were the after-opening window
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The central trap here: an unopened claim can run to a year or more while an opened window is measured in weeks, a difference of roughly twentyfold between two true statements about the same bag. A page saying it stays fresh for months without saying unopened is misleading while being literally defensible.

insufficient_evidence.form: one number covering both whole bean and ground on a page selling both
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Ground coffee's window is materially shorter because more surface area is exposed, so a single figure is wrong for one of the two offers.

insufficient_evidence.form: "stays fresh for months" with no qualifier
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Neither the open state nor the grind state is specified, so the claim cannot be applied to any actual purchase.

insufficient_evidence.form: a packaging-derived figure quoted without its precondition
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Valve and gas-flush figures depend on the pack being intact and are properties of the packaging rather than of the coffee.

insufficient_evidence.form: "won't expire" offered as a freshness statement
insufficient_evidence.why_not: That is a safety statement, and the trade association that makes it pairs it with a moisture and mould caveat.

conflict_rules.when: the page sells ground coffee and states only one undifferentiated window
conflict_rules.resolution: record that the stated window is not differentiated for the ground state, which is the check the readable grind option makes possible

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Almost no page separates opened from unopened or differentiates by grind state, so the assertion as specified would fail for nearly everyone. Published as advisory because the underlying confusion is real and worth naming, not because the row should be run.

entries.consumer_note: An unopened bag and an opened one have wildly different useful lives, and a page quoting one figure is usually quoting the flattering one. If you buy ground, expect roughly half the window of whole bean.
entries.merchant_remediation: State two windows with units — unopened and after opening — and differentiate them for each grind state you sell, rather than carrying one figure across every offer.

citations.source: National Coffee Association, storage and shelf life guidance
citations.establishes: materially shorter windows than specialty marketing implies — one to two weeks for ground and one to three for whole beans at room temperature — and that unopened packages retain freshness until the best-by date, which is a different anchor entirely

citations.source: America's Test Kitchen
citations.establishes: the consumer-facing separation of quality from safety: flavour deteriorates after two to three weeks while the beans remain safe for months, which is why a safety statement cannot answer a freshness question

refutation.challenged: Whether shelf-life duration is shopper-driven or a trade preoccupation.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass placed roast date, shelf life and storage together inside the verified shopper-driven core on live search-intent evidence and independently verified the trade association's one-to-three versus one-to-two week split. The entry stays advisory because no external definition exists to check any stated number against.

entries.question: Will this be roasted after I order, and how soon after roasting does it ship?

applicability.applies_when: the seller makes a roast-to-order or freshness-at-dispatch claim
applicability.signal: product or policy text claims roasting on demand
