accepted_evidence.form: a stated maximum interval between roasting and dispatch with units, plus a roast schedule and an order cut-off making it auditable

insufficient_evidence.form: "ships within 24 hours"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The cleanest and most common trap in the freshness class: it is dispatch latency, not roast age. A bag roasted three weeks ago also ships within twenty-four hours, so any check matching a short interval near freshness language accepts a statement that constrains nothing.

insufficient_evidence.form: "roasted to order" unqualified
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It describes the workflow rather than the latency and is compatible with the next scheduled batch being days away.

insufficient_evidence.form: "we roast Mondays" with no dispatch commitment
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A Monday roast dispatched Friday loses four days, and the schedule alone conceals that.

insufficient_evidence.form: a subscription cadence read as a roast-to-delivery bound
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Delivery every two weeks says nothing about the age of the coffee in any one delivery.

insufficient_evidence.form: express or free two-day shipping
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Courier speed is substituted for roast recency, which is the substitution this entry exists to refuse.

insufficient_evidence.form: a roast-to-order claim on a page where no roast date reaches the buyer
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The promise is then structurally unfalsifiable, because the buyer has no way to check the thing they were sold on.

conflict_rules.when: the only quantified interval on the page is a shipping interval
conflict_rules.resolution: refuse the freshness reading; the tractable check here is negative rather than positive

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Very few sellers commit to a roast-to-dispatch maximum with a cut-off, while many make an unqualified roast-to-order claim, so the assertion as specified would fail for nearly all of them. Its value is in distinguishing the two rather than in the pass rate.

entries.consumer_note: Ships within twenty-four hours tells you when the parcel leaves, not how old the coffee is. The claim worth looking for names a maximum time between roasting and dispatch, and it is only checkable if the bag that arrives carries its roast date.
entries.merchant_remediation: State a maximum roast-to-dispatch interval with units alongside your roast schedule and order cut-off, and print the roast date on the bag so the commitment can be checked.

citations.source: Shopify App Store listing for a coffee roasting-schedule application
citations.establishes: that roast-to-order fulfilment is a real tooled operational pattern on the platform this standard targets, with software existing to turn incoming orders into roasting schedules — so the claim describes a genuine workflow rather than only a marketing posture

refutation.challenged: Whether the buyer-community evidence for roast-to-dispatch was ever actually read, as opposed to cited by thread title.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass found that the entire case rested on forum threads whose contents neither the researcher nor the refuter could retrieve, because the forums block automated access. The demand claim is therefore weaker than the research presented, the entry is advisory, and the citation retained is the platform tooling rather than the unread threads.

entries.question: If I choose the ground option, when is it actually ground?

applicability.applies_when: the page offers a ground option
applicability.signal: a purchasable ground or brew-specific grind option exists

accepted_evidence.form: a statement of when grinding occurs relative to order and dispatch, together with a freshness window stated for the ground state

insufficient_evidence.form: a grind dropdown with no statement of when grinding happens
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The commonest shape, and it silently inherits whatever freshness copy was written for whole bean.

insufficient_evidence.form: "ground fresh to order"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: In practice this usually means ground at pack time within the same batch, so the roast date is unchanged while the freshness clock is roughly halved, and the page almost never says so.

insufficient_evidence.form: the whole-bean freshness window quoted where the selected variant is ground
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The two states have materially different windows, so the figure is wrong for the offer being bought.

insufficient_evidence.form: the roast date offered as the answer
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A bag ground on day one and one ground on day twenty share a roast date and are not equivalent products.

insufficient_evidence.form: a grind named only by brew method
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Grind size drives the degassing rate, and method names do not pin a particle size.

conflict_rules.when: the page sells a ground option and states only a whole-bean window
conflict_rules.resolution: record the undifferentiated window as the finding; the readable grind option is what makes this check possible at all

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Grind timing is essentially never stated, so this would fail for almost every page offering a ground option. It is published because the asymmetry it exposes is genuinely useful: the grind option is machine-readable while the grind date is not, which converts an unreadable question into a readable structural check.

entries.consumer_note: Ground coffee stales faster than beans, so when it was ground matters as much as when it was roasted. Ground fresh to order usually means ground when the bag was packed rather than when you ordered.
entries.merchant_remediation: State when grinding happens relative to dispatch, and give a freshness window for the ground state rather than reusing the whole-bean figure.

citations.source: Smrke and others, Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry
citations.establishes: that the degassing rate of ground coffee depends strongly on grind size and roast temperature and less on roast degree, so ground is not one state and a coarse and an espresso grind of the same lot do not behave alike

citations.source: National Coffee Association, storage and shelf life guidance
citations.establishes: the shorter room-temperature window for ground coffee against whole beans, and the surface-area mechanism behind it

refutation.challenged: Whether shoppers ask when the coffee was ground, or whether this is inferred from the beans-versus-ground discussion.
refutation.resolution: The research itself marked the demand as inferred rather than directly evidenced, which is why the entry is advisory. What survives independently is the structural observation that a page selling a ground option and stating only a whole-bean window is making an undifferentiated claim.

entries.question: Does the bag have a one-way valve to let the gas out?

applicability.applies_when: the product is roasted coffee in a bag

accepted_evidence.form: an explicit statement that this product's packaging includes a one-way degassing valve, attached to the size actually being sold

insufficient_evidence.form: "airtight", "resealable", "zip-lock", "tin tie"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: These are closures rather than valves, a valved bag with no zipper and a resealable bag with no valve are both common, and a tin tie is documented as not airtight.

insufficient_evidence.form: a product photograph appearing to show a valve
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Image content is not read, is frequently a stock or lifestyle shot, and often shows a different size or an older bag design.

insufficient_evidence.form: a valve claimed on the brand's packaging page but not on this product
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Valve presence commonly varies by size within one brand, so a site-level claim does not establish a fact about this offer.

insufficient_evidence.form: "keeps coffee fresh" or "oxygen barrier"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Outcome and film claims rather than the valve, and the two are different mechanisms.

insufficient_evidence.form: "vacuum sealed"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A vacuum pack and a valved pack are different and largely incompatible approaches.

conflict_rules.when: a closure and a valve are both mentioned
conflict_rules.resolution: record them separately; conflating closure with valve is the specific confusion this entry exists to catch

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Valve presence is rarely stated per product even where the bag has one, so the assertion would fail for most pages. It is published mainly so that the closure-versus-valve confusion is named, which is the part of this question a machine can genuinely check.

entries.consumer_note: A one-way valve lets carbon dioxide out without letting oxygen in, and only works while the seal is intact. It tells you nothing about how old the coffee is, so it is not a substitute for a roast date.
entries.merchant_remediation: If the pack for this size has a one-way valve, say so on the product page and keep it distinct from resealability, which is a different feature.

citations.source: Perfect Daily Grind
citations.establishes: the documented function of a one-way degassing valve and the precondition that defeats the claim, namely that the bag must be completely sealed for it to be effective — and separately that a tin tie is not airtight while a zipper creates a seal

refutation.challenged: Whether buyers ask about valve presence before purchase at all.
refutation.resolution: The research volunteered that it found no buyer thread asking for valve presence pre-purchase and recorded the demand as trade-taught rather than shopper-originated. The refuting pass agreed, placing the whole packaging tier among the classes to cut and noting that three of its four entries refute themselves. This entry survives only as advisory, and only because the closure-versus-valve confusion is a checkable defect.

entries.question: Is this coffee shade grown, and is that the same as bird friendly?

applicability.applies_when: the page makes a shade-grown, bird-friendly or habitat claim
applicability.signal: shade or habitat language in product text

accepted_evidence.form: the farm on the certifier's public certified-farms list, the importer on its certified-importers list, or the roaster and this named product in its buy-online directory
the named scheme and the current mark, distinct from generic shade language

insufficient_evidence.form: "shade grown", "canopy grown", "grown under native shade"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: None is the certification, and this is the highest-volume near-miss in coffee because it describes exactly the practice the certification measures.

insufficient_evidence.form: a different sustainability seal offered as equivalent
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The main alternative scheme has no shade requirement at all, so the substitution swaps a real habitat claim for a weaker and different one.

insufficient_evidence.form: an older version of the mark
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Superseded seals remain in circulation, so the mark's version is part of what a reader has to check.

insufficient_evidence.form: a certified farm named while the roaster holds no seal-use agreement
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The certifier requires a signed agreement plus periodic volume reporting from the roaster, so farm certification alone does not authorise a seal on a retail bag.

insufficient_evidence.form: "supports migratory birds" or donation language
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A contribution is not a habitat property of this coffee.

insufficient_evidence.form: absence from the public list read as absence of certification
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The lists carry no dates or status fields, so a match is good evidence while a non-match is no evidence.

conflict_rules.when: the roaster appears in the buy-online directory but this product does not
conflict_rules.resolution: record the roaster-level match and state that it does not reach this product, because the directory names specific products

registry.register_name: Smithsonian Migratory Bird Center Bird Friendly certified-farms, certified-importers and buy-online directories
registry.operator: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
registry.lookup_key: farm or producer name, importer name, or roaster and product name
registry.lookup_method: Three curated public HTML lists, free and filterable, covering certified coffee farms, certified importers, and a buy-online directory naming specific roasters and products. No certificate numbers, no certification dates, no status field, no last-updated stamp, no API and no bulk download.
registry.notes: Unusually, the buy-online directory names specific products, making this one of very few coffee claims a machine could in principle resolve to a named product from a public source — but with no IDs, dates or status, a match proves listing rather than current certification.

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Very few coffee pages carry this specific scheme, while generic shade language is common, so an assertion demanding the scheme would fail for nearly every page making a habitat claim. Published as advisory so the shade-versus-scheme distinction is on record.

entries.consumer_note: Shade grown describes a farming practice that no one audits; the habitat scheme that does audit it maintains public lists of certified farms, importers and even specific products you can search yourself. The better-known green seal has no shade requirement.
entries.merchant_remediation: Name the habitat scheme and use its current mark rather than generic shade language, and where you hold a seal-use agreement, make the certified farm or importer identifiable so a reader can find it in the public lists.

citations.source: National Audubon Society, how to choose a bird-friendly coffee
citations.establishes: that consumer guidance directs shoppers to look for specific seals and to visit the certifier's website to find where to buy, which is demonstrable shopper-side use of a certification as a purchase key

citations.source: Coffee & Conservation, guide to coffee certifications
citations.establishes: that the main alternative scheme has no shade-management criteria and does not require shade cover for years, so certified coffee under it may not be shade grown — the substitution a shopper is most likely to make

citations.source: Smithsonian's National Zoo, guidance for importers, roasters and distributors
citations.establishes: that farms hold the certification while importers and roasters obtain seal-use rights by legal agreement with periodic volume reporting, which is why a certified farm does not authorise a roaster's on-pack seal

refutation.challenged: Whether any certification question survives the finding that certificate auditing is trade rather than shopper behaviour.
refutation.resolution: This is the one that survives. The refuting pass cut the certificate-verification tier as trade-invented but named shade-grown and bird-friendly as the exception, because independent conservation and consumer-guide sources genuinely instruct shoppers here. It also confirmed the registers resolve farms rather than roasters and carry no status field, which is why the entry is advisory rather than blocked-pending-a-lookup.

entries.question: What variety is this, and can a Geisha claim be checked?

applicability.applies_when: the page names a coffee variety
applicability.signal: a variety name in product text

accepted_evidence.form: a variety name that resolves in the published varieties catalogue, attributed to this lot, ideally with the producer so the seed source is traceable

insufficient_evidence.form: "Geisha" or "Gesha" with nothing else
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Independent conformity work on plant material found a high rate of misidentification, so the bare name is weak evidence even of good faith.

insufficient_evidence.form: "heirloom" treated as a variety
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It is not a variety; it is an admission that the variety is unidentified, so a check that accepts it credits an absence as a presence.

insufficient_evidence.form: a catalogue link presented as verification
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The catalogue proves the variety exists and describes it; it says nothing about whether this bag contains it, and its own lookup method confirms that.

insufficient_evidence.form: "Gesha-influenced", "Gesha type", "Panamanian-style Geisha"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Deliberately unfalsifiable hedges that borrow the name's value without making its claim.

insufficient_evidence.form: "Arabica" offered as a variety
insufficient_evidence.why_not: That is a species, not a variety, and it is true of almost all specialty coffee.

insufficient_evidence.form: a competition result for a different lot from the same farm
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A farm's other lots are not this lot, and this is the highest-yield near-miss because the farm genuinely did place.

conflict_rules.when: the page names a variety and the origin's material is generally unidentified
conflict_rules.resolution: record the stated name; saying the variety is not identified is the honest and checkable alternative for such origins

registry.lookup_method: A public reference catalogue of variety descriptions and agronomic data. It resolves whether a variety NAME exists and what it is; it has no seller, brand, product or lot lookup and cannot authenticate a bag. Genetic identity requires shipping beans to a laboratory at material cost.
registry.notes: Recorded as not resolvable despite a real public catalogue existing, because the catalogue answers a question about the variety rather than about the product.

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Specialty single-origin pages name a variety often and blends and mainstream listings almost never, so a genuine split exists. The band is a hypothesis about seller populations and the assertion could only ever check that a name is stated.

entries.consumer_note: Variety is a real and interesting fact and an unverifiable one from a page: the public catalogue tells you what a variety is, not whether your bag contains it. For the most valuable names, independent work on plant material has found misidentification is common.
entries.merchant_remediation: Name the variety and the producer so the seed source can be traced, and where the variety is genuinely unknown say so, which is more useful than a catch-all name.

citations.source: World Coffee Research varieties catalogue
citations.establishes: that a public reference catalogue of coffee varieties exists with agronomic descriptions, and — by containing no product, brand or lot lookup — that it cannot authenticate a retail claim

refutation.challenged: Whether variety is a shopper question and whether the catalogue makes the claim registry-resolvable as the research asserted.
refutation.resolution: Both challenges landed. The refuting pass confirmed the catalogue is a variety-name reference with no seller, brand, SKU or lot lookup, so it cannot authenticate a bag and the research's own stated lookup method contradicted its own status label. It also placed the specialty-provenance tier as largely trade-invented, and noted that the misidentification figure concerns nursery and seed-lot plant material rather than retail bags. The entry is advisory and its registry block records resolvable as false.

entries.question: Is there a cupping score, and does it come with enough detail to mean anything?

applicability.applies_when: the page states a cupping score or a specialty grade
applicability.signal: a numeric score or grade claim in product text

accepted_evidence.form: a score with its protocol, its evaluator and its date, or a green-grading result stated in the protocol's own terms with the sample mass named

insufficient_evidence.form: a score with no protocol, cupper or date
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A score is a measurement and a measurement without its method is not evidence, because run-to-run and cupper-to-cupper variation is real.

insufficient_evidence.form: "specialty coffee" as a category word
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It names a market segment rather than a grade, and no defect result accompanies it.

insufficient_evidence.form: "Q graded" with no grader named and no report
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The credential belongs to a person, so citing it without the person is unverifiable.

insufficient_evidence.form: an origin grade offered as evidence of a cupping score
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Origin grades encode bean size or altitude bands assigned at export, which is a different system with a different criterion.

insufficient_evidence.form: "premium", "gourmet", "top one per cent"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: No body defines these, so they resolve against nothing.

insufficient_evidence.form: a defect count with no sample mass, or one mass compared against another without conversion
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Counts are only comparable on a stated basis, and the protocols differ in the mass they use.

insufficient_evidence.form: last season's score carried over to this lot
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A score belongs to the lot that was cupped, and a new harvest is a new lot.

conflict_rules.when: an in-house score is presented in a form resembling a formal protocol result
conflict_rules.resolution: record the score and the absence of a named protocol and evaluator; the standard reports what is stated rather than ranking the source

registry.notes: Competition results are published for competition lots, which is a small fraction of coffee and does not constitute a register of scores.

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Scores appear on a minority of pages and almost never with protocol, evaluator and date, so the assertion as specified would fail for nearly all of them. Published as advisory because the bare-number form is worth naming as insufficient rather than because the row should be run.

entries.consumer_note: A cupping score is a measurement by a person under a protocol on a particular day, and a bare number carries none of that. Two cuppers and two sessions can differ, so a score without its method is closer to a slogan than a specification.
entries.merchant_remediation: Publish the score with the protocol, the evaluator and the date, and keep it attached to the lot it was measured on rather than to the product across seasons.

citations.source: Specialty Coffee Association, coffee standards index
citations.establishes: that the published trade standards cover sensory assessment protocols and evaluator competencies, which is what makes protocol, evaluator and sample mass the elements a stated score needs in order to be interpretable

refutation.challenged: Whether cupping scores are a shopper question at all.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass placed cupping scores inside the specialty-provenance tier it recommended cutting, on the grounds that the sources define terms rather than evidence demand. The entry is retained as advisory because a bare score is a common and misleading page element worth naming, and its demand basis carries a trade-convention warning label rather than claiming buyer evidence.

entries.question: If I do not like the coffee, can I send it back after I have opened the bag?

applicability.applies_when: the product is a consumable sold to a consumer at distance

accepted_evidence.form: an explicit statement of whether an opened bag may be returned, with the window, the mechanism and the remedy
the same statement attached to this product

insufficient_evidence.form: a thirty-day returns window with no statement about opened product
insufficient_evidence.why_not: For a durable good the window is the policy; for a consumable it is half the policy, and the missing half decides every real case — you cannot know you dislike coffee without opening it.

insufficient_evidence.form: "satisfaction assured" or "not happy? let us know"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Discretionary goodwill with no window, no mechanism, no remedy and no obligation.

insufficient_evidence.form: "contact us within 30 days"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A duty to ask is not a right to a refund.

insufficient_evidence.form: store credit presented as a refund
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A credit is not a return of the price paid, and where a statutory cancellation right applies it does not discharge it.

insufficient_evidence.form: structured returns data asserting a window while the linked policy excludes opened goods
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The machine-readable field and the prose disagree, and a check reading only the field passes a policy that is effectively void for this category.

insufficient_evidence.form: "for food safety and hygiene reasons we cannot accept returns of opened products"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It reads as a statement of law and, for sealed shelf-stable roasted coffee sold to an EU or UK consumer, is likely wrong on both available exceptions: the coffee does not deteriorate rapidly, and the hygiene exception addresses goods sealed for health protection with a seal the bag does not carry.

conflict_rules.when: structured data and the policy prose disagree on the window
conflict_rules.resolution: record both and report the disagreement; the standard does not decide which governs

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Almost no policy addresses the opened-bag case explicitly, which is precisely why the question matters, so the assertion would fail for nearly everyone. Published as advisory because the substantive legal reading is contested and a standard should not assert a violation it cannot establish.

entries.consumer_note: A returns window that says nothing about opened bags leaves out the only case that arises for coffee. Where a seller cites food safety as the reason, that is often their policy rather than the law, and for sealed shelf-stable coffee an EU or UK cancellation right may still apply.
entries.merchant_remediation: State plainly whether an opened bag may be returned, with the window, the mechanism and whether the remedy is money or credit, rather than relying on a generic window.

citations.source: EU Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU, Articles 6, 16(d) and 16(e)
citations.establishes: that the trader must inform the consumer of the cancellation right before the contract, and that the exceptions relied on for food cover goods liable to deteriorate rapidly and goods sealed for health protection whose seal has been broken — neither of which plainly reaches sealed shelf-stable roasted coffee

refutation.challenged: Whether the reading that the food and hygiene exceptions do not cover sealed roasted coffee is defensible enough to publish.
refutation.resolution: It is defensible and not settled, so the entry is advisory and its wording says the seller's reasoning is likely wrong rather than that it is unlawful. The commercial-terms mandates in this class were separately confirmed by the refuting pass as genuine web-page obligations, unlike the food-labelling rules corrected elsewhere in this standard.

entries.question: If I subscribe, can I cancel online myself, where I signed up?

applicability.applies_when: the page offers a recurring purchase option
applicability.signal: a subscription or recurring option on the page

accepted_evidence.form: a named cancellation mechanism in the same place the buyer signs up, with any cut-off stated
the same mechanism described in the terms attached to the offer

insufficient_evidence.form: "cancel anytime"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The near-miss that will fool every keyword check. The whole premise of the regulation in this area is that the phrase is printed constantly and not honoured; it names no mechanism, no location and no cut-off, and it is fully consistent with a flow requiring a phone call during business hours.

insufficient_evidence.form: "manage your subscription in your account"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Managing is not cancelling; many portals offer only skip, pause, delay and swap.

insufficient_evidence.form: "pause or skip anytime" where cancel is absent
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Deferring a shipment is not ending the commitment.

insufficient_evidence.form: "contact us to cancel" framed as convenience
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It relocates the mechanism to a channel the seller controls and can queue.

insufficient_evidence.form: a cancel link that opens a retention flow with no terminal cancel
insufficient_evidence.why_not: An offer to stay is not a mechanism to leave.

insufficient_evidence.form: a claim of compliance with a click-to-cancel rule
insufficient_evidence.why_not: The federal rule most often named was vacated, so a compliance claim naming it refers to a rule that does not exist and should be read as a warning sign rather than as evidence.

conflict_rules.when: the subscription selector is injected client-side and the terms are server-rendered
conflict_rules.resolution: record that the offer terms could not be read from the page as served rather than that they are absent

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: A named self-serve mechanism with a cut-off is rare while the unqualified phrase is near-universal, so the assertion would fail for nearly every page offering a subscription. Its value is entirely in refusing the phrase rather than in the pass rate.

entries.consumer_note: Cancel anytime is the phrase regulators built rules around because it is printed constantly and often not honoured. What matters is whether the page names where and how you cancel, and whether there is a cut-off before the next shipment.
entries.merchant_remediation: Name the cancellation mechanism and its location in the same place the buyer subscribes, state any cut-off, and make the flow terminate in an actual cancellation rather than in a retention offer.

citations.source: US Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act, 15 USC 8403
citations.establishes: that a negative-option seller must provide simple mechanisms to stop recurring charges and must disclose material terms before obtaining billing information, which makes the cancellation mechanism a regulated web-page element

refutation.challenged: Whether the subscription-complaint statistic underpinning this class could be verified, and whether a vacated rule was being cited as live law.
refutation.resolution: The complaint statistic could not be verified anywhere by the refuting pass, including in the legal alert the research leaned on, so it is not cited here. The research had already correctly recorded that the federal click-to-cancel rule was vacated rather than treating struck-down law as live, and the refuting pass credited that; this entry cites the underlying statute instead and treats a compliance claim naming the vacated rule as a warning sign.

entries.question: If this ships to my country, who pays the customs duty and import tax?

applicability.applies_when: the seller offers international shipping
applicability.signal: international shipping offered in policy or checkout terms

accepted_evidence.form: a statement of which party bears duty and import tax, scoped to the destinations it applies to

insufficient_evidence.form: "we ship worldwide"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: No destination list and no duty statement, and frequently untrue at checkout.

insufficient_evidence.form: "taxes and duties calculated at checkout"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: This describes a process rather than a term and does not say who ends up paying; it is the single most common way the question is dodged while appearing answered.

insufficient_evidence.form: "free shipping over a threshold" where the threshold is domestic only
insufficient_evidence.why_not: A check extracting a zero shipping rate records free international shipping, which is the opposite of the term.

insufficient_evidence.form: "prices exclude taxes"
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It states neither what will be added nor by whom.

insufficient_evidence.form: a delivered-duty term with no country scope
insufficient_evidence.why_not: Such terms are typically offered on some lanes only, so an unscoped statement is not a term for the buyer's destination.

insufficient_evidence.form: a destination list with no duty term
insufficient_evidence.why_not: It satisfies structured-data validation while leaving the buyer exposed to the surprise the question is about.

conflict_rules.when: a duty statement predates a change in a destination's de minimis treatment
conflict_rules.resolution: treat the statement as suspect for that destination and record its scope rather than accepting it as current

predicted_discrimination.reasoning: Most sellers offering international shipping describe a process rather than stating who bears duty, so the assertion would fail for a large majority. Published as advisory because the checkout-time dodge is worth naming and because scoping the term by destination is beyond what a product page usually carries.

entries.consumer_note: Duty and import tax on a coffee parcel can arrive as a demand at the door, and calculated at checkout does not tell you who pays. The term you want names the party and the destinations it covers.
entries.merchant_remediation: State who bears duty and import tax, scoped to the destinations the term covers, in the shipping policy rather than deferring the answer to checkout.

citations.source: Baymard Institute checkout usability research
citations.establishes: that unexpected costs added at or after checkout are among the leading measured causes of cart abandonment, which is the documented consequence of leaving duty incidence unstated

refutation.challenged: Whether the abandonment figures cited for this question were verifiable and whether the question is coffee-specific.
refutation.resolution: The refuting pass verified the abandonment research figures and placed cost transparency including duty inside the verified shopper-driven core. It is not coffee-specific, which is why it is advisory here rather than a headline assertion, and it is retained because coffee is a low-value, frequently cross-border parcel where a duty demand is disproportionate to the order.
